StsBasilGreg.about: Basil and Gregory were friends from Cappadocia, in what is now Turkey, who studied together in Athens and then gave themselves to prayer and the service of the Church. Basil became Bishop of Caesarea in 370. He wrote rules for monastic life that still guide the monks of the East, built a large hospice for the poor and the sick, and defended the divinity of Christ and of the Holy Spirit against the Arians. Gregory, a reluctant bishop and a gifted preacher, served for a short time as Bishop of Constantinople and is known in the East as “the Theologian” for his teaching on the Trinity.

NameJesus.about: The name Jesus means “God saves”. The angel gave it to Mary at the Annunciation, before the child was conceived, and later to Joseph in a dream, “for he will save his people from their sins”. Saint Paul teaches that at this name every knee should bend. Devotion to the Holy Name spread widely in the fifteenth century through the preaching of the Franciscans Saint Bernardine of Siena and Saint John of Capistrano, who promoted the monogram IHS. A feast was extended to the whole Church in 1721, and the present optional memorial was restored to the calendar in 2002.

StElizabethSeton.about: Elizabeth Ann Bayley was born in New York into an Episcopalian family, married William Seton and had five children. Her husband died in Italy in 1803, and the faith of the Catholic friends who sheltered her there drew her to the Church, which she entered in 1805. Left with little money and shunned by many relatives, she opened a school in Baltimore and in 1809 founded the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph at Emmitsburg, Maryland. Her sisters taught poor children and helped lay the foundations of Catholic schooling in the United States. Canonised in 1975, she was the first native-born citizen of that country to be declared a saint.

StJohnNeumann.about: John Neumann was born at Prachatice in Bohemia, now in the Czech Republic. Wishing to serve as a missionary, he sailed to New York in 1836 and was ordained there the same year. After some years working among immigrant settlers in the west of New York State he joined the Redemptorists. In 1852 he became Bishop of Philadelphia, where he built many churches, organised the first diocesan system of Catholic schools in the United States, and promoted the Forty Hours devotion before the Blessed Sacrament. Small in stature and simple in his ways, he travelled constantly to visit his people. He died in 1860 and was canonised in 1977.

StAndreBessette.about: Alfred Bessette was born into a poor family in Quebec and had lost both parents by the age of twelve. Frail and barely able to read, he was accepted with some hesitation by the Congregation of Holy Cross, took the name André, and served for about forty years as doorkeeper of a college in Montreal. He welcomed the sick and troubled who came to him, prayed with them, and urged them to turn to Saint Joseph. Many reported healings, which he always attributed to the saint. With gifts from ordinary people he began a small chapel on Mount Royal that grew into Saint Joseph’s Oratory. He was canonised in 2010.

StRayPenyafort.about: Raymond was born near Barcelona, taught law at Bologna, and entered the Dominican Order in 1222, when he was already in middle age. Pope Gregory IX called him to Rome and asked him to gather the scattered laws of the Church into a single collection, the Decretals, which remained the basis of canon law until 1917. He also wrote a guide for confessors that was used for centuries. Elected Master of the Dominicans in 1238, he resigned after two years and spent the rest of his long life in Spain, preaching, hearing confessions, and encouraging missions among Jews and Muslims. He died at about one hundred years of age.

StHilaryPoitiers.about: Hilary was born at Poitiers in Gaul to a pagan family and came to the Christian faith as an adult through reading the Scriptures. He was a married man when the people chose him as their bishop about the year 350. At that time many bishops, backed by the emperor, accepted the Arian teaching that the Son is not truly God. Hilary resisted and was exiled to Phrygia in Asia Minor, where he wrote his principal work, on the Trinity. Allowed home after some years, he continued to teach and to reconcile those who had wavered. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1851.

StAnthonyEgypt.about: Anthony was born in Egypt to prosperous Christian parents. When he was about twenty he heard in church the Gospel words “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor”, and took them as spoken to him. He gave away his property and went to live in solitude, first near his village and then deep in the desert, in prayer, manual work and a long struggle against temptation. Others came to live near him and learn from him, and so he is called the father of monks. Saint Athanasius, who knew him, wrote his life. He died in 356, aged about 105.

StFabianPope.about: Fabian was Bishop of Rome from 236 to 250. The historian Eusebius relates a story that he had newly arrived from the country and was chosen when a dove settled on his head as the people gathered to elect a pope. He governed during a time of peace, is said to have divided the city into seven districts under seven deacons for the care of the poor, and saw to the burial places of the martyrs. When the Emperor Decius began a general persecution, Fabian was among the first to die, in January 250. He was buried in the catacomb of Saint Callistus, where his gravestone was found.

StSebastian.about: Sebastian was martyred in Rome, probably during the persecution of Diocletian near the end of the third century, and was buried on the Appian Way, where the basilica bearing his name now stands. Saint Ambrose says that he came from Milan. Little else is certain. According to a later account, he was an officer of the imperial guard who used his position to encourage Christians in prison. When this was discovered he was shot with arrows and left for dead, recovered, confronted the emperor, and was then beaten to death. He has been honoured in Rome since at least the fourth century.
StSebastian.patron: Patron of soldiers, athletes and archers

StAgnes.about: Agnes was a Roman girl of twelve or thirteen who was put to death for her faith, most likely in the persecution of Diocletian at the start of the fourth century. Saint Ambrose and other early writers tell that she had consecrated her virginity to Christ, refused offers of marriage, and went to her death without fear. She was buried beside the Via Nomentana, where a basilica was built over her tomb within a few decades. Her name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Each year on her feast two lambs are blessed in Rome, and their wool is woven into the pallia given to new metropolitan archbishops.

StVincentDeacon.about: Vincent was a deacon of Saragossa in Spain who served and preached on behalf of his bishop, Valerius. During the persecution of Diocletian both were arrested and taken to Valencia. The bishop was sent into exile, but Vincent was tortured and died of his wounds in prison about the year 304. His fame spread quickly through the whole Church. The poet Prudentius wrote a hymn in his honour, and Saint Augustine, preaching on his feast, remarked that Vincent was celebrated wherever the Roman Empire or the Christian name had reached. He is the best known of the early martyrs of Spain.

PrayerUnborn.about: In the dioceses of the United States, 22 January, or 23 January when the 22nd falls on a Sunday, is kept as a day of prayer for the full restoration of the legal guarantee of the right to life, and of penance for offences against the dignity of the human person committed through abortion. The date is the anniversary of the 1973 Supreme Court decision in Roe v. Wade, which made abortion legal throughout the country and which the Court overturned in 2022. The Mass may be offered in thanksgiving for the gift of human life, in white vestments, or for peace and justice, in violet.

StMarianneCope.about: Barbara Koob was born in Germany in 1838 and grew up in Utica, New York, where she worked in a factory to support her family before joining the Sisters of Saint Francis of Syracuse. As Mother Marianne she helped to found two hospitals and led her congregation. In 1883 she answered an appeal from Hawaii for sisters to nurse people with leprosy, and went there with six companions. In 1888 she moved to the settlement at Kalaupapa on Molokai, where she cared for Saint Damien in his last months and carried on his work, running homes for girls and boys. She died there in 1918 and was canonised in 2012.

StFrancisDeSales.about: Francis was born into a noble family in Savoy and studied at Paris and took a doctorate in law at Padua before becoming a priest in 1593. He volunteered for a difficult mission in the Chablais region, where by patient preaching and leaflets slipped under doors he won many Calvinists back to the Catholic faith. As Bishop of Geneva from 1602, living at Annecy, he was known for his gentleness. His Introduction to the Devout Life taught that holiness is for people in every state of life. With Saint Jane Frances de Chantal he founded the Order of the Visitation. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1877.

ConversionStPaul.about: Saul of Tarsus was a zealous Pharisee who approved the killing of Saint Stephen and set out for Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus. On the road a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” It was the risen Lord, who identifies himself with his Church. Blinded, Saul was led into the city, where Ananias restored his sight and baptised him. The persecutor became the Apostle to the Gentiles. This feast has been kept in the West since the early Middle Ages, and it closes the yearly Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

StsTimothyTitus.about: Timothy and Titus were close companions of Saint Paul, honoured on the day after the feast of his conversion. Timothy came from Lystra in Asia Minor, the son of a Greek father and a Jewish mother, Eunice, who with his grandmother Lois taught him the Scriptures. He travelled with Paul and, according to tradition, became the first Bishop of Ephesus. Titus was a Gentile convert whom Paul took to Jerusalem, sent as his envoy to the troubled Church in Corinth, and left in Crete to appoint elders in every town. Three letters of the New Testament are addressed to them, giving counsel on the care of the Christian community.

StAngelaMerici.about: Angela was born at Desenzano on Lake Garda in northern Italy and lost her parents while young. She became a Franciscan tertiary and, troubled by how little instruction girls received in the faith, began to gather and teach them. In 1535 at Brescia she and a group of companions formed the Company of Saint Ursula. Its members did not withdraw into a convent or wear a habit, but lived with their own families, consecrated to God and devoted to the Christian formation of girls. From it grew the Ursulines, the first order of women dedicated to education. Angela died in Brescia in 1540.

StThomasAquinas.about: Thomas was born near Aquino, between Rome and Naples, and schooled by the Benedictines of Monte Cassino. Against strong opposition from his noble family he joined the Dominicans. He studied under Saint Albert the Great and taught at Paris and in Italy. In his Summa Theologiae and many other works he set out the Catholic faith drawing on Scripture, the Fathers and the philosophy of Aristotle, confident that faith and reason cannot contradict each other. He also wrote the hymns for the feast of Corpus Christi. He died in 1274 on his way to the Council of Lyons, and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1567.
StThomasAquinas.patron: Patron of students, schools and universities

StJohnBosco.about: John Bosco was born to a poor farming family in Piedmont, northern Italy and lost his father at the age of two. Ordained in 1841, he went to Turin, where the growth of industry had drawn many boys who lived on the streets or ended up in prison. He gathered them for Mass, catechism and games, then opened workshops, schools and a home. He believed in guiding the young by reason, religion and kindness rather than punishment. To continue the work he founded the Salesians in 1859, named after Saint Francis de Sales, and with Saint Mary Mazzarello the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians. He was canonised in 1934.
StJohnBosco.patron: Patron of young people and apprentices

Presentation.about: Forty days after his birth, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the Temple in Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as the Law of Moses required for a firstborn son. There the aged Simeon, moved by the Holy Spirit, took the child in his arms and called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles”, and the prophetess Anna spoke of him to all who were waiting for redemption. The feast was kept in Jerusalem in the fourth century and reached Rome by the seventh. Candles are blessed and carried in procession, which gives the day its old name of Candlemas.

StAnsgar.about: Ansgar was born in northern France, became a monk at Corbie, and later taught at its daughter house of Corvey in Germany. In 826 he went as a missionary to Denmark, and a few years later to Sweden, where he founded the first Christian community at the trading town of Birka. He was made the first Archbishop of Hamburg, and when Vikings destroyed that city in 845 he carried on from Bremen. Much of what he built was swept away by raids and by a return to paganism, yet he began again each time. He died at Bremen in 865 and is called the Apostle of the North.

StBlase.about: Blase was Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, now Sivas in Turkey, and was martyred about the year 316. Nothing more is known with certainty. Later accounts say that he was a physician before he became bishop, that he hid in a cave during the persecution, and that on his way to prison he healed a boy who was choking on a fish bone. From this comes the custom of blessing throats on his feast, when the priest holds two crossed candles to the throat of each person and asks God, through the intercession of Saint Blase, to deliver them from illness of the throat and every other evil.
StBlase.patron: Patron of those who suffer from illnesses of the throat

StAgatha.about: Agatha was martyred at Catania in Sicily, probably in the persecution of the Emperor Decius about the year 251. Devotion to her spread quickly, and her name is included in the Roman Canon of the Mass. The details of her story come from later accounts and cannot be verified. According to these, she was a young woman of good family who had dedicated herself to Christ, refused the advances of a Roman official, and was cruelly tortured, her breasts being cut off, before she died in prison. The people of Catania have long asked her protection against the eruptions of Mount Etna.
StAgatha.patron: Patron of Catania and of those who suffer from diseases of the breast

StsPaulMiki.about: On 5 February 1597 twenty-six Christians were crucified on a hill at Nagasaki in Japan by order of the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi. They were six Franciscan missionaries, three Japanese Jesuits, and seventeen Japanese lay people, among them three boys. They had been arrested around Kyoto and Osaka and marched hundreds of miles through the winter. Paul Miki, a Jesuit preparing for the priesthood and a gifted preacher, spoke from his cross, declaring that he died for the Gospel and forgave those who put him to death. They were the first martyrs of Japan, canonised in 1862. The Church there later survived in secret for more than two centuries without priests.

StJeromeEmiliani.about: Jerome was born in Venice in 1486 and became a soldier. Taken prisoner in 1511 while defending a fortress, he turned to prayer in his cell and attributed his release to the help of Our Lady. When famine and plague struck northern Italy in 1528 he nursed the sick and took orphaned children into his own house. He went on to found orphanages in several cities, where the children learned a trade as well as the faith. The companions who joined him became the Somascan Fathers, named after the village of Somasca where he settled. He died there in 1537 of a disease caught from the sick.
StJeromeEmiliani.patron: Patron of orphans and abandoned children

StJosephineBakhita.about: Bakhita was born about 1869 in Darfur in Sudan. As a small girl she was kidnapped by slave traders, who gave her the name Bakhita, meaning “fortunate”. She was sold several times and treated with great cruelty. An Italian consul bought her in Khartoum and took her to Italy, where she served a family as a nursemaid. With the Canossian Sisters in Venice she came to know Christ, and in 1889 an Italian court confirmed that she was free. She was baptised Josephine in 1890 and became a Canossian sister, serving for decades as cook and doorkeeper at Schio. She died in 1947 and was canonised in 2000.
StJosephineBakhita.patron: Patron of Sudan and of victims of human trafficking

StScholastica.about: Scholastica was the sister of Saint Benedict, born at Nursia in central Italy about 480, and consecrated to God from her youth. All that is known of her comes from Saint Gregory the Great. He tells that she lived near Monte Cassino and met her brother once a year to speak of the things of God. At their last meeting she begged him to stay the night. When he refused, she prayed, and so violent a storm arose that he could not leave. Three days later she died, and Benedict saw her soul rise to heaven like a dove. He buried her in the tomb prepared for himself.

OurLadyOfLourdes.about: Between 11 February and 16 July 1858, the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared eighteen times to Bernadette Soubirous, a poor girl of fourteen, at a grotto beside the river Gave at Lourdes in southern France. The Lady asked for prayer and penance for sinners and for a chapel to be built, and showed Bernadette a spring. On 25 March she gave her name: “I am the Immaculate Conception”, four years after that dogma was defined. The local bishop judged the apparitions worthy of belief in 1862. Lourdes has become a place of pilgrimage for the sick, and this day is also kept as the World Day of the Sick.

StsCyrilMethodius.about: Cyril and Methodius were brothers from Thessalonica, where they learned the language of the neighbouring Slavs. In 863 the Emperor in Constantinople sent them to Moravia, in central Europe, whose prince had asked for teachers who could preach in his people’s tongue. They devised an alphabet for the Slavonic language and translated the Gospels and the liturgy into it. Opposed by some who thought only Latin, Greek and Hebrew fit for worship, they went to Rome, where the Pope approved their work. Cyril died there in 869. Methodius returned as archbishop and laboured on, despite imprisonment, until 885. Saint John Paul II named them co-patrons of Europe in 1980.

SevenHolyFounders.about: About the year 1233 seven prosperous merchants of Florence, members of a lay confraternity devoted to Our Lady, left their businesses and homes to live together in prayer, poverty and penance. Seeking greater solitude they withdrew to Monte Senario, in the hills north of the city. Others asked to join them, and the group became the Order of Servants of Mary, known as the Servites, following the Rule of Saint Augustine and marked by devotion to the sorrows of Mary at the foot of the cross. The last survivor, Alexis Falconieri, who chose to remain a lay brother, died on 17 February 1310. The seven were canonised together in 1888.

StPeterDamian.about: Peter was born at Ravenna in 1007, was orphaned early and owed his education to an older brother. He became a successful teacher, then left it all about 1035 to join the hermits of Fonte Avellana, where he later served as prior. His writing and preaching called the clergy of his day back to prayer, poverty and chastity, and he spoke out against the buying and selling of Church offices. Against his wishes he was made Cardinal Bishop of Ostia in 1057 and served several popes as a legate and peacemaker. He died at Faenza in 1072 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1828.

ChairStPeter.about: This feast honours not a piece of furniture but the office that Christ gave to Peter when he said, “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church.” A bishop’s chair, or cathedra, is the sign of his authority to teach, and the chair of Peter stands for the mission of the Pope, as Peter’s successor, to confirm his brothers and sisters in the faith and to keep the Church in unity. The feast was already kept in Rome on 22 February in the fourth century. An ancient wooden chair long venerated as Peter’s is enshrined in Bernini’s bronze monument in the apse of Saint Peter’s Basilica.

StPolycarp.about: Polycarp was Bishop of Smyrna, now Izmir in Turkey, and one of the last links with the Apostles. Saint Irenaeus, who heard him as a boy, says he had been taught by Saint John. He welcomed Saint Ignatius of Antioch on his way to martyrdom, and travelled to Rome to discuss the date of Easter with the Pope. About the year 155 he was arrested and told to curse Christ. He answered that he had served him for eighty-six years and had never been wronged by him. The account of his death in the stadium, written by his own Church, is the oldest of its kind to survive.

StGregoryNarek.about: Gregory was an Armenian monk and priest who spent nearly all his life in the monastery of Narek, near Lake Van in what is now eastern Turkey, where he taught and wrote. His best known work is the Book of Lamentations, a collection of ninety-five prayers addressed to God from the depths of the heart. In them he speaks as a sinner on behalf of all people, confident in God’s mercy. Armenian Christians have treasured the book for a thousand years and often simply call it the Narek. Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church in 2015 and placed his memorial in the General Roman Calendar in 2021.

StKatharineDrexel.about: Katharine Drexel was born in Philadelphia in 1858, the daughter of a wealthy and devout banker. Moved by the poverty of Native Americans and African Americans, she asked Pope Leo XIII in 1887 to send missionaries to them. He suggested that she become one herself. In 1891 she founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament, and over the following decades she spent her large inheritance on schools and missions across the country, among them Xavier University of Louisiana in New Orleans. After a heart attack in 1935 she lived nearly twenty years in quiet prayer. She died in 1955 and was canonised in 2000.

StCasimir.about: Casimir was born in Kraków in 1458, a younger son of Casimir IV, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania. At court he chose a life of prayer and simplicity, often spending part of the night before the Blessed Sacrament, and was generous to the poor. At thirteen he was sent with an army to claim the throne of Hungary. The venture failed, and he would not take part in such a war again. He later governed Poland for a time in his father’s absence and remained unmarried, having given himself to God. He died of a lung disease in 1484, aged twenty-five, and is buried in Vilnius.

StsPerpetuaFelicity.about: Perpetua and Felicity were put to death in the arena at Carthage in North Africa on 7 March 203. Perpetua was a young married woman aged about twenty-two, with an infant son. Felicity was a slave, who gave birth to a daughter in prison days before she died. Both were preparing for baptism when they were arrested with several companions, and they were baptised while in custody. Perpetua kept a record of her imprisonment, her father’s pleas that she give up her faith, and her visions. It is one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. Their names are in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

StJohnGod.about: John was born in Portugal in 1495 and spent many years in Spain as a shepherd, a soldier and a seller of books. When he was past forty, a sermon by Saint John of Avila in Granada moved him so deeply that his public displays of repentance had him confined for a time in a hospital for the insane, where he saw how badly the sick were treated. On his release he rented a house and began to take in the sick poor, begging for what they needed. Others joined him and after his death became the Brothers Hospitallers of Saint John of God. He died in Granada in 1550.
StJohnGod.patron: Patron of hospitals, the sick and nurses

StFrancesRome.about: Frances was born in Rome in 1384 to a noble family. She wished to be a nun, but in obedience to her parents married Lorenzo Ponziani while very young. Their marriage lasted forty years, and she was a devoted wife and mother, who suffered the death of children and the loss of property in the wars that troubled the city. With her sister-in-law she nursed the sick and fed the poor. In 1425 she founded a community of women oblates attached to the Benedictines and devoted to prayer and the service of the poor. After her husband’s death she went to live with them, and died in 1440.
StFrancesRome.patron: Patron of Benedictine oblates and of motorists

StPatrick.about: Patrick was born in Roman Britain late in the fourth century, the son of a deacon. At sixteen he was seized by raiders and taken to Ireland, where he spent six years as a slave herding animals and learned to pray. He escaped and reached home, but later felt called in a dream to return to the people who had enslaved him. He went back as a bishop, traditionally in 432, and spent the rest of his life preaching, baptising and ordaining clergy. Two short writings of his survive, the Confession and a letter protesting against the enslavement of his converts by the soldiers of a British chieftain.

StCyrilJerusalem.about: Cyril was born about 315 and became Bishop of Jerusalem about 350. He is remembered chiefly for the instructions he gave to those preparing for baptism at Easter, delivered in the church built over the tomb of Christ. These Catecheses explain the Creed and the sacraments of Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist, and show how the Church in Jerusalem prayed in the fourth century. His years as bishop were troubled by the disputes over Arianism, and he was driven into exile three times. He took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381, which completed the Creed said at Mass. Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church.

StJoseph.about: Joseph, a carpenter of Nazareth and a descendant of King David, was the husband of the Virgin Mary and the guardian of the child Jesus. The Gospel calls him a just man. Told by an angel in a dream that Mary’s child was conceived by the Holy Spirit, he took her as his wife, gave the child his name, led the family to safety in Egypt, and brought them home to Nazareth, where Jesus grew up under his care. No word of his is recorded. He is thought to have died before Jesus began his public ministry. Blessed Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church in 1870.
StJoseph.patron: Patron of the Universal Church, of fathers, of workers and of a happy death

StTuribius.about: Turibius was born in Spain in 1538 and studied law at Salamanca. He was a layman serving as a judge at Granada when King Philip II chose him to be Archbishop of Lima. He was ordained, and reached Peru in 1581. He spent years crossing his vast diocese on foot and by mule, learning the local languages so that he could teach and hear confessions without an interpreter. He defended the native peoples against the abuses of the colonists, held councils to reform the clergy, and founded one of the first seminaries in the Americas. He confirmed Saint Rose of Lima. He died while on a visitation in 1606.
StTuribius.patron: Patron of the bishops of Latin America

Annunciation.about: Nine months before Christmas the Church celebrates the moment when the Son of God took flesh. Saint Luke tells that the angel Gabriel was sent to Mary at Nazareth and announced that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son, Jesus, the Son of the Most High. Mary answered that she was the handmaid of the Lord and consented to God’s word. So the Word became flesh in her womb. The feast was kept in the East by the sixth century and then in Rome. When 25 March falls in Holy Week or Easter Week, it is moved to the Monday after the Second Sunday of Easter.

StFrancisPaola.about: Francis was born in 1416 at Paola in Calabria, in southern Italy. As a youth he withdrew to a cave near his home town to live as a hermit, and others soon joined him. From this beginning grew the Order of Minims, whose name means “the least”, and whose members bound themselves to humility, penance and a perpetual Lenten fast. His reputation for holiness and miracles spread so far that King Louis XI of France, close to death, asked the Pope to send him. Francis lived in France for his remaining twenty-four years and died near Tours on Good Friday 1507. He was canonised in 1519.
StFrancisPaola.patron: Patron of seafarers and of Calabria

StIsidore.about: Isidore was born about 560 into a family that gave the Church in Spain four saints. He succeeded his brother Leander as Bishop of Seville around 600 and led the diocese for more than thirty years. He worked to bring the Visigoths, who had been Arian, fully into the Catholic faith, presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, and urged that schools for the clergy be set up in every diocese. His best known work, the Etymologies, gathered the learning of the ancient world into a single encyclopaedia used throughout the Middle Ages. He died in 636 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1722.

StVincentFerrer.about: Vincent Ferrer was born at Valencia in Spain in 1350 and joined the Dominicans as a young man. He lived through the Western Schism, when rival claimants to the papacy divided the Church, and for years he supported the claimant at Avignon in good faith. From 1399 he travelled on foot through Spain, France, Switzerland and northern Italy, preaching repentance and the coming judgement to great crowds, and many were converted. In the end he withdrew his support from the Avignon claimant, which helped to bring the schism to a close. He died at Vannes in Brittany in 1419 and was canonised in 1455.

StJohnBaptistDeLaSalle.about: John Baptist de la Salle was born at Reims in France in 1651 into a wealthy family and became a priest and cathedral canon. Drawn into helping a group of schoolmasters who taught poor boys, he gave up his position and his fortune to live among them, and formed them into the Brothers of the Christian Schools. He had children taught together in classes rather than one by one, used French in place of Latin, and opened colleges to train teachers. He met much opposition, and died at Rouen on Good Friday 1719. He was canonised in 1900, and in 1950 Pius XII named him patron of teachers.

StStanislaus.about: Stanislaus was born about 1030 at Szczepanów in southern Poland and became Bishop of Kraków in 1072. He was known as a preacher and a generous friend of the poor. When King Bolesław II acted with cruelty and injustice, the bishop rebuked him and at last excommunicated him. In 1079 the king had him killed; according to tradition Bolesław struck him down with his own hand while Stanislaus was celebrating Mass in a chapel outside the city. The king lost his throne soon afterwards. Stanislaus was canonised in 1253, and his tomb in the cathedral on the Wawel hill in Kraków is a national shrine.

StMartinPope.about: Martin was born at Todi in Umbria and was elected Pope in 649. The emperors at Constantinople then favoured the teaching that Christ had only one will, a divine one, and had forbidden further discussion. Martin called a council at the Lateran, which taught that Christ, being truly God and truly man, has both a divine and a human will. For this the Emperor Constans II had him seized in 653 and carried to Constantinople, where he was tried and condemned. He was exiled to the Crimea and died there in 655, worn out by ill treatment. He is the last Pope to be honoured as a martyr.

StAnselm.about: Anselm was born about 1033 at Aosta in the Alps. He became a monk at the abbey of Bec in Normandy, where he became abbot and wrote the works that made him one of the leading thinkers of the Middle Ages. He described his task as “faith seeking understanding”: beginning from belief, he used reason to explore what the Church holds about God and about why God became man. In 1093 he was made Archbishop of Canterbury. He defended the Church’s freedom against two English kings and was twice driven into exile. He died at Canterbury in 1109 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1720.

StAdalbert.about: Adalbert, baptised Vojtěch, was born about 956 into a noble family at Libice in Bohemia. He became Bishop of Prague while still a young man, but met such resistance to his efforts at reform that he twice left his diocese and lived as a monk in Rome. Unable to return to Prague, he went as a missionary, with the support of the Polish duke Bolesław the Brave, to the pagan Prussians on the Baltic coast. There he was killed on 23 April 997. Bolesław ransomed his body and buried it at Gniezno, and he was canonised two years later.

StGeorge.about: Little is known for certain about George beyond the fact that he died for Christ, probably about the year 303 during the persecution of the Emperor Diocletian, and was buried at Lydda in Palestine. According to tradition he was a soldier in the Roman army who refused to give up his faith. His tomb drew pilgrims from an early date, and devotion to him spread throughout East and West. The well-known story of his killing a dragon to save a king’s daughter is a later legend, often read as an image of the victory of faith over evil. He is patron of England and of many other countries and cities.
StGeorge.patron: Patron of England and of soldiers

StFidelisSigmaringen.about: Mark Roy was born at Sigmaringen in southern Germany about 1577. He practised as a lawyer and took the cases of those who could not pay, so that he was called the poor man’s advocate. Troubled by dishonesty in the courts, he left the law, was ordained priest and joined the Capuchin friars in 1612, taking the name Fidelis, which means “faithful”. He was sent to preach in the Grisons region of Switzerland, where many had become Calvinist, for the newly founded Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith. On 24 April 1622 he was killed by armed men at Seewis after preaching there. He was canonised in 1746.

StMarkEvangelist.about: Mark is the author of the second Gospel, the shortest of the four and probably the earliest. He is usually identified with the John Mark of the Acts of the Apostles, whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the first Christians. He set out with Paul and his cousin Barnabas on their first missionary journey, and was later with both Paul and Peter in Rome; Peter calls him “my son”. Early tradition holds that his Gospel records Peter’s preaching, and that he founded the Church at Alexandria in Egypt and died there as a martyr. His relics have been venerated in Venice since the ninth century.

StLouisGrignionMontfort.about: Louis-Marie Grignion was born in 1673 at Montfort in Brittany and was ordained priest in 1700. He spent his short life preaching parish missions across western France, calling people back to their baptismal promises, teaching the rosary and caring for the poor and the sick. He founded two congregations, the Daughters of Wisdom and the Company of Mary. His book True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin, found long after his death, teaches that giving oneself wholly to Mary is a sure way of belonging to Jesus. Saint John Paul II took his motto, “Totus tuus”, from it. Louis died in 1716 and was canonised in 1947.

StPeterChanel.about: Peter Chanel was born in 1803 into a farming family in eastern France. Ordained in 1827, he served as a country priest and then joined the newly formed Marists. In 1836 he sailed with the first Marist missionaries to the Pacific and was put ashore on the island of Futuna. For more than three years he learned the language, tended the sick and won respect by his patience, though few asked for baptism. When the chief’s son sought to become a Christian, the chief had Peter clubbed to death on 28 April 1841. Within a few years the whole island was Catholic. He is the first martyr of Oceania.

StCatherineSiena.about: Catherine was born at Siena in 1347, one of the youngest of a large family. She vowed herself to Christ as a girl and while still young became a lay member of the Dominican order, living at home in prayer and penance and then nursing the sick and the plague-stricken. Though she had little schooling, she dictated hundreds of letters and a book, the Dialogue, and became an adviser to rulers and popes. She pressed Pope Gregory XI to leave Avignon and return to Rome, which he did in 1377. She died in Rome in 1380, aged thirty-three. She was named a Doctor of the Church in 1970.
StCatherineSiena.patron: Patron of Italy and co-patron of Europe

StPiusV.about: Antonio Ghislieri was born in 1504 near Alessandria in northern Italy, of a poor family, and entered the Dominicans at fourteen, taking the name Michele. Elected Pope in 1566, he set himself to carry out the reforms of the Council of Trent. He published the Roman Catechism, a revised Breviary and, in 1570, the Roman Missal that remained in use for four centuries. He lived simply, as a friar, and cared personally for the poor and sick of Rome. He helped to form the alliance of Christian states whose fleet defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto in 1571, a victory he attributed to the rosary. He died in 1572.

StJosephWorker.about: Pope Pius XII established this memorial in 1955, placing it on 1 May, kept in many countries as a holiday of labour. It honours Saint Joseph as the craftsman of Nazareth, who supported Mary and Jesus by the work of his hands and taught his trade to the Son of God; in the Gospel Jesus is known as “the carpenter’s son”. The memorial sets before the Church the dignity of human work, by which men and women share in God’s work of creation, provide for their families and serve their neighbour. It is a fitting day to pray for all who work, and for those who cannot find work.

StAthanasius.about: Athanasius was born in Alexandria in Egypt about 296. As a young deacon he went with his bishop to the Council of Nicaea in 325, which taught that the Son is truly God, of one substance with the Father, against the priest Arius who denied it. Three years later he became Bishop of Alexandria, and for forty-five years he defended the faith of Nicaea against emperors and bishops who favoured Arianism. He was driven from his see five times and spent about seventeen years in exile. His writings include On the Incarnation and a life of Saint Anthony of Egypt that spread the monastic ideal. He died in 373.

StsPhilipJames.about: Philip came from Bethsaida in Galilee, the town of Peter and Andrew. In John’s Gospel he brings Nathanael to Jesus, and at the Last Supper he asks, “Lord, show us the Father.” James, the son of Alphaeus, is named in every list of the Twelve. The Western tradition has identified him with James, “the brother of the Lord”, who led the Church in Jerusalem, is linked with the Letter of James, and was put to death there about the year 62. The two apostles share a feast because their relics were placed together in the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles in Rome, which was dedicated in the sixth century.

StJohnAvila.about: John was born about 1499 at Almodóvar del Campo in central Spain. After studying at Salamanca and Alcalá he was ordained priest, gave his inheritance to the poor and hoped to go as a missionary to the New World. His bishop kept him instead in southern Spain, where his preaching earned him the name Apostle of Andalusia. He founded colleges, worked for the better training of priests, and guided many by his letters, among them Saint John of God, Saint Francis Borgia and Saint Teresa of Avila. His chief book is Audi, filia. He died in 1569, was canonised in 1970 and named a Doctor of the Church in 2012.
StJohnAvila.patron: Patron of the diocesan clergy of Spain

StDamienVeuster.about: Jozef De Veuster was born in 1840 to a farming family in Belgium. He joined the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary, taking the name Damien, and was sent to Hawaii, where he was ordained in 1864. On 10 May 1873 he arrived, at his own request, at the settlement on Molokai where people with leprosy were confined. For sixteen years he was their priest, and also their builder, nurse and gravedigger, bringing order and hope to an abandoned community. He contracted the disease himself and died of it in 1889. He was canonised in 2009. His memorial falls on the day he landed on Molokai.

StPancras.about: Pancras was a young Christian put to death in Rome, probably about the year 304 during the persecution of Diocletian. According to tradition he was an orphan from Phrygia in Asia Minor who had been brought to Rome by his uncle, became a Christian there, and was beheaded at the age of fourteen for refusing to sacrifice to the Roman gods. He was buried beside the Via Aurelia, where a basilica bearing his name still stands. Devotion to him spread widely. The missionaries sent from Rome to England carried it with them, and one of the first churches built at Canterbury was dedicated to him.

StsNereusAchilleus.about: Nereus and Achilleus were Roman martyrs buried in the catacomb of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina, where a basilica was built over their tomb in the fourth century. The oldest record of them is a verse inscription by Pope Damasus, who died in 384. It says that they were soldiers who had carried out the cruel orders of a tyrant, were converted to Christ, threw away their weapons and left the camp, and gladly gave their lives for the faith. When they died is not known. A later legend makes them servants of Flavia Domitilla, a Christian noblewoman of the emperor’s family, but that account is not regarded as historical.

OurLadyOfFatima.about: Between 13 May and 13 October 1917, three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, reported that the Blessed Virgin appeared to them six times near Fatima in Portugal, most often at the Cova da Iria. She asked for prayer, especially the daily rosary, for penance, for the conversion of sinners and for devotion to her Immaculate Heart, and spoke of peace for a world then at war. In 1930 the local bishop judged the apparitions worthy of belief. Francisco and Jacinta, who died in childhood, were canonised in 2017. The memorial was added to the General Roman Calendar in 2002.

StMatthiasAp.about: After the Ascension, the apostles met to choose someone to take the place of Judas among the Twelve. Peter laid down that it must be one who had been with them the whole time, from the baptism of John until the day Jesus was taken up, so as to be a witness to the resurrection. Two men were put forward, Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias. The community prayed and cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias. Scripture says nothing further of him, and later traditions about where he preached and how he died do not agree. His feast usually falls in Eastertide, close to the events it recalls.

StIsidoreFarmer.about: Isidore was born in Madrid, probably about 1070, to poor parents, and spent his whole life as a hired labourer on the land of a wealthy landowner, Juan de Vargas. He is said to have gone to Mass each morning before work and to have prayed as he followed the plough. He and his wife, María, who is also venerated in Spain, shared what little they had with those poorer than themselves. He died about 1130. In 1622 he was canonised together with Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Avila and Philip Neri. He is the patron of Madrid and of farmers and rural communities.
StIsidoreFarmer.patron: Patron of farmers and of Madrid

StJohnIPope.about: John was a Tuscan who was elected Pope in 523, when he was already old and frail. Italy was then ruled by Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, who was an Arian. When the Emperor Justin in Constantinople took measures against the Arians in the East, Theodoric forced the Pope to lead an embassy to have them reversed. John was received with great honour, the first Pope to visit Constantinople, and celebrated Easter there. He could not, however, obtain all that the king demanded. On his return Theodoric, suspecting him of plotting with the emperor, imprisoned him at Ravenna, where he died of ill treatment on 18 May 526.

StBernardineSiena.about: Bernardine was born in 1380 at Massa Marittima in Tuscany, of a Sienese family, and was orphaned as a child. As a young man he ran a hospital in Siena during an outbreak of plague. He joined the Franciscans in 1402 and for decades travelled the length of Italy on foot, preaching in the open air to crowds too large for any church. He spoke plainly against feuding, gambling and usury, and urged devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, holding up a tablet bearing the letters IHS. He also led a renewal of stricter observance among the friars. He died at L’Aquila in 1444 and was canonised in 1450.

StChristopherMagallanes.about: This memorial honours twenty-five martyrs of Mexico, twenty-two diocesan priests and three laymen, who were killed between 1915 and 1937, most of them in the years after 1926 when the government enforced harsh laws against the Church and public worship was suspended. Cristóbal Magallanes, born in 1869, was parish priest of Totatiche in the state of Jalisco, where he founded schools and a small seminary after others had been closed. Arrested on his way to say Mass, he was shot without trial on 25 May 1927 with his fellow priest Agustín Caloca. Saint John Paul II canonised the group on 21 May 2000.

StRitaCascia.about: Rita was born about 1381 at Roccaporena near Cascia in Umbria. According to tradition she wished to become a nun but was married young to a harsh-tempered man and bore him two sons. After some eighteen years her husband was murdered in a local feud. Rita forgave his killers and prayed that her sons would not seek revenge; both died soon afterwards. She was then admitted to the Augustinian convent at Cascia, where she lived some forty years in prayer and penance. She is said to have borne on her forehead a wound like that of a thorn from Christ’s crown. She died in 1457 and was canonised in 1900.

StBedeVenerable.about: Bede was born about 673 in the north of England and at seven was entrusted to the monks of Wearmouth. He spent the rest of his life there and at its sister house at Jarrow, praying, studying, teaching and writing. Most of his work was commentary on Scripture, but he is best known for his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in 731, the chief source for the coming of Christianity to England. He died in 735 on the eve of the Ascension; a pupil’s account says he had just finished dictating a translation of Saint John’s Gospel. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1899.

StGregoryVII.about: Hildebrand was born in Tuscany about 1020 and came to Rome as a boy. He served a succession of reforming popes before being elected himself in 1073, taking the name Gregory. He worked to free the Church from control by lay rulers, forbidding the buying and selling of church offices and the practice by which kings and princes invested bishops with their office. This brought him into conflict with the German king Henry IV, whom he excommunicated and who came as a penitent to Canossa in 1077. The struggle was renewed, Henry seized Rome, and Gregory died in exile at Salerno in 1085. He was canonised in 1606.

StMaryMagdalenePazzi.about: Caterina de’ Pazzi was born in 1566 into one of the leading families of Florence. At sixteen she entered the Carmelite monastery of Santa Maria degli Angeli in that city, taking the name Mary Magdalene. During a serious illness early in her religious life she began to experience ecstasies, and what she said in them was written down by her sisters. These graces were followed by years of darkness, temptation and physical suffering, which she bore with patience. She had a burning desire for the renewal of the Church and offered her prayer and hidden life for that end. She died in 1607 and was canonised in 1669.

StPhilipNeri.about: Philip Neri was born in Florence in 1515 and came to Rome as a young man. For years he lived there as a layman, praying in the catacombs, visiting the sick and talking about God with people in the streets and shops. Ordained in 1551, he spent long hours hearing confessions and gathered round him a circle who met for prayer, spiritual reading and music. From these meetings grew the Congregation of the Oratory, approved in 1575. His cheerfulness and gentleness won many back to the practice of the faith, and he came to be called the Apostle of Rome. He died in 1595 and was canonised in 1622.

StAugustineCanterbury.about: Augustine was prior of the monastery of Saint Andrew in Rome when Pope Gregory the Great chose him in 596 to lead some forty monks to preach the Gospel to the English. They landed in Kent in 597. King Ethelbert, whose wife Bertha was already a Christian, received them kindly, gave them a place to live in Canterbury and was himself baptised, and many of his people followed. Augustine was consecrated bishop and made Canterbury his see, becoming its first archbishop. He founded a monastery there and set up further bishoprics at London and Rochester. He died on 26 May, about the year 604.

StPaulVI.about: Giovanni Battista Montini was born in 1897 near Brescia in northern Italy and was ordained priest on 29 May 1920, the date on which his memorial is kept. After long service of the Holy See he became Archbishop of Milan in 1954 and was elected Pope in 1963. He guided the Second Vatican Council to its close in 1965 and oversaw the reforms that followed, including that of the liturgy. He was the first Pope of modern times to travel widely, beginning with a pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 1964. His encyclicals include Populorum Progressio and Humanae Vitae. He died in 1978 and was canonised in 2018.

Visitation.about: This feast recalls the journey Mary made, soon after the Annunciation, to the hill country of Judah to visit her kinswoman Elizabeth, who was expecting a child in her old age. Saint Luke tells that at Mary’s greeting the unborn John the Baptist leapt in his mother’s womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, called Mary blessed among women. Mary answered with the song of praise known as the Magnificat. The feast was kept by the Franciscans from 1263 and was extended to the whole Western Church in 1389. Since 1969 it has been celebrated on 31 May, between the Annunciation and the birth of John the Baptist.

StJustinMartyr.about: Justin was born about the year 100 at Flavia Neapolis, the modern Nablus, in Samaria, to a pagan family. He searched for truth among the schools of Greek philosophy and found it at last in Christianity, becoming a Christian about 130. He went on wearing the philosopher’s cloak and opened a school in Rome. His two Apologies, addressed to the emperor and the senate, defend Christians against false charges and give one of the earliest descriptions of baptism and the Sunday Eucharist. Denounced to the authorities, he refused to sacrifice to the gods and was beheaded with six companions about 165. The record of his trial survives.

StsMarcellinusPeter.about: Marcellinus, a priest, and Peter, an exorcist, were put to death in Rome about the year 304 during the persecution of Diocletian. Pope Damasus, who composed the verses for their tomb, wrote that as a boy he had heard the story from their executioner himself: they were taken to a lonely place outside the city and beheaded, so that their grave should remain unknown, but their bodies were later recovered and buried with honour. After the peace of the Church, the Emperor Constantine built a basilica over their tomb on the Via Labicana. Their names are included in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass.

StsCharlesLwanga.about: These twenty-two Catholics, most of them young pages at the court of Mwanga, king of Buganda, in what is now Uganda, were put to death between 1885 and 1887. Missionaries had brought the faith only a few years earlier. The king turned against the Christians, partly because the pages refused his immoral demands. Joseph Mukasa, a senior court official, was beheaded first. Charles Lwanga, who then cared for the pages and baptised several of them, was burned alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886, as were twelve other Catholics, among them Kizito, aged about fourteen. Anglican Christians died alongside them. Pope Paul VI canonised the martyrs in 1964.
StsCharlesLwanga.patron: Charles Lwanga is patron of African Catholic youth

StBoniface.about: Winfrid was born about 675 in the kingdom of Wessex in England and became a monk and teacher. In middle age he left England as a missionary. Pope Gregory II commissioned him in 719 to preach to the peoples east of the Rhine and gave him the name Boniface. For thirty-five years he preached in Hesse, Thuringia and Bavaria, founded monasteries including Fulda, established dioceses, and as archbishop helped to reform the Frankish Church, always in close union with Rome. In old age he returned to the mission in Frisia, where on 5 June 754 he and his companions were killed by pagans. He is buried at Fulda.

StNorbert.about: Norbert was born about 1080 at Xanten in the Rhineland to a noble family and lived for years as a worldly cleric at the imperial court. A narrow escape from death in a thunderstorm changed his life. He was ordained priest, gave away his property and became a travelling preacher. In 1120 he settled with a few companions at Prémontré in northern France, where they lived as canons under the Rule of Saint Augustine, combining common prayer with pastoral work. So began the Premonstratensian order, also called Norbertines. In 1126 he was made Archbishop of Magdeburg, where he worked for reform until his death in 1134.

StEphrem.about: Ephrem was born about 306 at Nisibis in Mesopotamia and served the Church there as a deacon and teacher. When Nisibis was handed over to Persia in 363 he moved with many other Christians to Edessa, where he spent his last ten years. He wrote in Syriac, and taught the faith above all through hymns and poems, which were sung in church and answered the false teachings of his day; many honour Our Lady. He came to be called the Harp of the Holy Spirit. He died in 373, shortly after organising relief for the victims of a famine. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1920.

StBarnabasAp.about: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, to whom the apostles gave the name Barnabas, “son of encouragement”. He sold a field and gave the money to the apostles. He vouched for the newly converted Paul before the wary Christians of Jerusalem, and later fetched him from Tarsus to help the growing Church at Antioch. The two were sent out together on the first missionary journey, to Cyprus and Asia Minor, and spoke at the council in Jerusalem for the freedom of Gentile converts. Though not one of the Twelve, he is called an apostle in Acts. Tradition holds that he was martyred in Cyprus.

StAnthonyPadua.about: Anthony was born in Lisbon in 1195 and baptised Fernando. He first joined the Augustinian canons, but the martyrdom of five Franciscans in Morocco moved him to become a friar in 1220. Illness ended his own mission to Morocco, and his ship home was driven to Sicily. In Italy his gifts as a preacher were discovered by chance, and Saint Francis approved his teaching theology to the brothers. He preached in northern Italy and southern France with deep knowledge of Scripture, and defended the poor against moneylenders. He died near Padua in 1231 and was canonised within a year. He was named a Doctor of the Church in 1946.
StAnthonyPadua.patron: Patron of the poor and of those seeking lost things

StRomuald.about: Romuald was born at Ravenna about 951 into a noble family. As a young man he saw his father kill a relative in a quarrel over property, and entered the nearby monastery of Sant’Apollinare in Classe to do penance. Seeking a stricter life, he left to live as a hermit under an older solitary. For the rest of his life he moved about Italy, founding and reforming monasteries and hermitages. The best known is Camaldoli in the Tuscan mountains, from which the Camaldolese take their name. They combine the solitude of the hermit with the common life of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Romuald died in 1027.

StAloysiusGonzaga.about: Aloysius was born in 1568, the eldest son of the Marquis of Castiglione in northern Italy, and was brought up to be a soldier and a prince. Amid the luxury and violence of the courts where he served as a page, he resolved to give his life to God. Against his father’s long opposition he gave up his inheritance to his brother and entered the Jesuits in Rome in 1585. When plague broke out in the city in 1591 he worked in the hospitals, carrying the sick on his own back, and fell ill himself. He died on 21 June that year, aged twenty-three. He was canonised in 1726.
StAloysiusGonzaga.patron: Patron of young people and students

StPaulinusNola.about: Paulinus was born about 354 near Bordeaux into one of the wealthiest families of Roman Gaul. He was well educated, held high public office and married a Spanish Christian, Therasia. After his baptism and the death of their only child in infancy, the couple began to give away their estates to the poor. Paulinus was ordained priest and they settled at Nola near Naples, beside the tomb of Saint Felix, living a monastic life and building a hospice for pilgrims and the needy. About 409 he was chosen as bishop of Nola. His poems and letters survive, including exchanges with Saint Augustine and Saint Jerome. He died in 431.

StsJohnFisherThomasMore.about: John Fisher, born in 1469, was a scholar, Chancellor of the University of Cambridge and for over thirty years Bishop of Rochester. Thomas More, born in London in 1478, was a lawyer, the author of Utopia, a devoted husband and father, and Lord Chancellor of England. When King Henry VIII set aside his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and had himself declared head of the Church in England, both men refused to take the oath required of them and were imprisoned in the Tower of London. Fisher, named a cardinal while in prison, was beheaded on 22 June 1535, and More on 6 July. They were canonised together in 1935.
StsJohnFisherThomasMore.patron: Thomas More is patron of statesmen and politicians

NativityJohnBaptist.about: The Church keeps the birthday of only three persons: the Lord, his Mother and John the Baptist. Saint Luke tells how the angel Gabriel announced to the priest Zechariah that his elderly wife Elizabeth would bear a son, and how Zechariah, struck dumb for doubting, recovered his speech when he named the child John and praised God in the canticle called the Benedictus. John was sent to prepare the way for Christ, and Jesus said that no one born of woman was greater. The solemnity, known from the fourth century, falls six months before Christmas, since Luke says Elizabeth was six months with child at the Annunciation.

StCyrilAlexandria.about: Cyril was born about 376 and in 412 succeeded his uncle Theophilus as Bishop of Alexandria. He is remembered for defending the truth that Jesus Christ is one person, the Son of God made man, so that Mary, who bore him, is rightly called Mother of God. When Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople, rejected that title, Cyril opposed him in writing and, with the backing of Pope Celestine, presided at the Council of Ephesus in 431, which upheld it. He could be a combative leader, but his writings on the Incarnation have shaped the Church’s teaching ever since. He died in 444 and is honoured as a Doctor of the Church.

StIrenaeus.about: Irenaeus was born about 130, probably at Smyrna in Asia Minor, where as a boy he listened to the bishop, Saint Polycarp, who had known the apostle John. He came to Lyon in Gaul as a priest and became its bishop about 177. His great work, Against Heresies, answers the Gnostic teachers who claimed a secret knowledge. Against them he set the faith handed down openly from the apostles through the bishops, the unity of the Old and New Testaments, and the goodness of creation. An old tradition says he died a martyr about 202. In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, the Doctor of Unity.

StsPeterPaulAp.about: This solemnity honours together the two apostles on whose witness the Church of Rome is founded. Peter, a fisherman from Galilee, was chosen by Christ as the rock on which he would build his Church. Paul of Tarsus, once a persecutor, became the apostle to the Gentiles and carried the Gospel across the Roman world. Both died as martyrs in Rome under the Emperor Nero, between 64 and 67. According to tradition Peter was crucified and buried on the Vatican hill, and Paul was beheaded on the road to Ostia; basilicas stand over their tombs. Rome has kept their feast on 29 June since at least the fourth century.
StsPeterPaulAp.patron: Patrons of the city of Rome

FirstMartyrsRome.about: In July of the year 64 a great fire destroyed much of Rome. The Emperor Nero, to turn suspicion from himself, laid the blame on the Christians of the city. The Roman historian Tacitus records that a great number were arrested and put to death with mockery: some were sewn into animal skins and torn by dogs, others crucified, others burned as torches to light the emperor’s gardens at night. Pope Saint Clement, writing some thirty years later, also remembers them. Their names are unknown. This memorial, placed on the day after the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul, honours these first martyrs of the Church of Rome.

JuniperoSerra.about: Junípero Serra was a Franciscan friar from the island of Majorca who gave up a university chair to become a missionary. He sailed to Mexico in 1749 and worked there for nearly twenty years. In 1769, already in his fifties and troubled by a bad leg, he went north to California and founded the mission of San Diego, the first of nine he established along the coast. He died at Mission San Carlos in Carmel, where he is buried. Pope Francis canonised him in Washington in 2015, the first canonisation to take place in the United States.

StThomasAp.about: Thomas, also called Didymus, “the Twin”, was one of the twelve apostles. Saint John’s Gospel records that he was absent when the risen Lord first appeared to the others and would not believe until he had seen and touched the wounds. A week later Jesus stood before him, and Thomas answered, “My Lord and my God.” According to an ancient tradition he carried the Gospel as far as India and died there as a martyr; the Christians of Kerala still call themselves Saint Thomas Christians. The feast on 3 July recalls the transfer of his relics to Edessa.
StThomasAp.patron: Patron of India and of architects and builders

StElizabethPortugal.about: Elizabeth was a princess of Aragon, named after her great-aunt Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, and was married very young to King Denis of Portugal. She bore his unfaithfulness patiently, prayed daily, and spent her wealth on hospitals, orphans and the poor. More than once she made peace between her husband and their rebellious son, and between rival kings. After Denis died in 1325 she lived as a Franciscan tertiary beside the convent of Poor Clares at Coimbra. She died at Estremoz in 1336, having travelled there to prevent a war between her son and the King of Castile. She was canonised in 1625.

IndependenceDay.about: On 4 July 1776 the Continental Congress, meeting in Philadelphia, adopted the Declaration of Independence, and the United States keeps the anniversary as its national day. The Roman Missal for the dioceses of the United States provides a Mass for the occasion, in which the Church gives thanks for the blessings the country has received and asks God for peace, justice and true freedom for all its people. One Catholic, Charles Carroll of Carrollton, was among those who signed the Declaration. Christians are taught to love their country, to pray for those who govern, and to work for the common good.

StAnthonyZaccaria.about: Anthony Mary Zaccaria was born at Cremona in northern Italy and trained as a physician at Padua. Caring for the sick poor drew him towards the care of souls as well, and he was ordained priest in 1528. In Milan he founded the Clerics Regular of Saint Paul, known as the Barnabites, together with a congregation of sisters and a movement for married lay people, all aimed at renewing Christian life in a lax age. He drew much from the letters of Saint Paul and encouraged frequent Communion, adoration of the Blessed Sacrament and devotion to Christ crucified. He died worn out at thirty-six.

StMariaGoretti.about: Maria Goretti was the daughter of poor farm labourers who had moved to the marshlands near Nettuno, south of Rome. After her father died she kept house and minded the younger children while her mother worked in the fields. In July 1902, when she was eleven, a young neighbour, Alessandro Serenelli, tried to force himself on her. She resisted, telling him it was a sin, and he stabbed her many times. She died in hospital the next day, having forgiven him. Serenelli repented in prison and later lived as a helper in a Capuchin friary. Pius XII canonised her in 1950, with her mother present.

StAugustineZhaoRong.about: This memorial honours one hundred and twenty martyrs who died for the faith in China between 1648 and 1930. Eighty-seven were Chinese, among them children, parents, catechists, seminarians and priests; thirty-three were foreign missionaries, including bishops, priests and religious sisters. Many were killed during the Boxer Rising of 1900. Augustine Zhao Rong, who heads the list, was a soldier who escorted the imprisoned missionary Gabriel-Taurin Dufresse, later a bishop and martyr. Moved by his patience, Zhao Rong asked for baptism and was afterwards ordained priest. He was arrested and died in 1815 after cruel torture. Pope John Paul II canonised them together on 1 October 2000.

StBenedict.about: Benedict was born at Nursia in central Italy and sent to study in Rome, but left the city to seek God alone in a cave at Subiaco. Disciples gathered round him, and about 529 he founded the monastery of Monte Cassino. There he wrote his Rule, a short and moderate guide to community life built on prayer, work, obedience and humility, which became the pattern for monasteries throughout the West. What is known of his life comes from Saint Gregory the Great. Benedictine houses preserved learning and spread the faith across Europe, and Paul VI named him patron of Europe in 1964.

StHenry.about: Henry was born in Bavaria in 973 and educated by Saint Wolfgang, Bishop of Regensburg. He became Duke of Bavaria, then King of Germany in 1002, and was crowned Holy Roman Emperor by Pope Benedict VIII in Rome in 1014. He used his authority to support the reform of the Church, restoring dioceses, endowing monasteries and founding the see of Bamberg, where he is buried. His wife, Cunegund, is also venerated as a saint. Henry shows that public office and responsibility for others can be a path to holiness. He died in 1024 and was canonised in 1146.

StCamillusDeLellis.about: Camillus de Lellis was born in the Abruzzi region of Italy and spent his youth as a soldier of fortune with a ruinous passion for gambling. Penniless in his mid-twenties, he was converted while working for the Capuchins, but an incurable sore on his leg kept him from joining them. He went instead to nurse at the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome, where he saw how badly the sick were treated. Ordained priest in 1584, he gathered companions who became the Ministers of the Sick, wearing a red cross and bound to serve the sick even at the risk of their lives. He died in Rome in 1614.
StCamillusDeLellis.patron: Patron of the sick, nurses and hospitals

KateriTekakwitha.about: Kateri Tekakwitha was born in 1656 in a Mohawk village in what is now New York State, the daughter of a Mohawk chief and a Christian Algonquin mother. Smallpox killed her parents when she was four and left her scarred and weak-sighted. Taught by Jesuit missionaries, she was baptised at Easter 1676 and suffered scorn for it from her own people. The next year she made the long journey on foot to the Christian village of Kahnawake near Montreal, where she lived in prayer, penance and care of the sick and old until her death at twenty-four. Benedict XVI canonised her in 2012.
KateriTekakwitha.patron: Patron of ecology and of the indigenous peoples of North America

StBonaventure.about: Bonaventure was born at Bagnoregio in central Italy and entered the Franciscans as a young man. He studied and taught theology in Paris, where he was a contemporary of Saint Thomas Aquinas. Elected Minister General of the Franciscans in 1257, he guided the order for seventeen years with such wisdom that he is called its second founder, and he wrote a life of Saint Francis. His works, among them The Journey of the Mind to God, join deep learning to burning love, which earned him the title Seraphic Doctor. Made a cardinal in 1273, he died during the Council of Lyon the following year.

OurLadyOfMountCarmel.about: Mount Carmel, in the Holy Land, is the mountain where the prophet Elijah defended faith in the one God. Around the end of the twelfth century a group of hermits settled there, built a chapel in honour of Mary, and became known as the Brothers of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. From them grew the Carmelite order. According to Carmelite tradition, Our Lady appeared to Saint Simon Stock, an English prior general, in 1251 and gave him the brown scapular as a sign of her protection. The feast began among the Carmelites in the fourteenth century and was extended to the whole Church in 1726.

StApollinaris.about: Apollinaris is honoured as the first bishop of Ravenna, on the Adriatic coast of Italy. Little is known of him for certain. According to tradition he came from Antioch and was sent by Saint Peter to preach in Ravenna, where he worked for many years, was repeatedly beaten and driven out, and at last died from his sufferings. Historians place him rather later, perhaps in the second century. Saint Peter Chrysologus, one of his successors, preached in his honour as a martyr, and the sixth-century basilica of Sant’Apollinare in Classe, with its famous mosaics, was built at the place of his burial.

StLawrenceBrindisi.about: Lawrence was born at Brindisi in southern Italy and joined the Capuchin Franciscans at Verona as a youth. A gifted linguist, he knew the Bible in its original languages, and his preaching, steeped in Scripture, carried him across Italy, Germany, Bohemia and Spain. He founded Capuchin houses in central Europe, served as Minister General of his order, and was often employed by popes and princes as a peacemaker. In 1601 he rode as chaplain with the imperial army in Hungary, holding up a crucifix. He died in Lisbon in 1619 while on an embassy to the King of Spain. John XXIII named him a Doctor of the Church in 1959.

StMaryMagdalene.about: Mary of Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee, was one of the women who followed Jesus and provided for him and the Twelve; Saint Luke says that seven demons had gone out of her. She stood by the cross with Our Lady and saw where the body was laid. On Easter morning she came to the tomb, and Saint John tells how the risen Lord called her by name and sent her to tell the disciples. For this she has been called the apostle of the apostles. In 2016 Pope Francis raised her memorial to a feast, the same rank as those of the apostles.

StBridget.about: Bridget was born into a noble Swedish family about 1303. Married at a young age to Ulf Gudmarsson, she had eight children, one of whom was Saint Catherine of Sweden. After her husband’s death she gave herself wholly to prayer and penance, and founded the Order of the Most Holy Saviour, the Bridgettines, at Vadstena. In 1349 she went to Rome, where she spent most of the rest of her life caring for the poor and pilgrims and urging the popes to return from Avignon. Her Revelations, centred on the Passion of Christ, were widely read. She died in Rome in 1373, and is a co-patron of Europe.
StBridget.patron: Co-patron of Europe and patron of Sweden

StSharbelMakhluf.about: Youssef Makhlouf was born in 1828 in a mountain village of northern Lebanon and grew up poor, tending the family’s animals. At twenty-three he entered the Lebanese Maronite Order, taking the name Sharbel, and was ordained priest in 1859. After sixteen years at the monastery of Saint Maron at Annaya he was allowed to withdraw to its nearby hermitage, where he lived for twenty-three years in silence, fasting, manual work and long prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. He was taken ill while celebrating Mass and died on Christmas Eve 1898. Many healings are attributed to his prayers. Paul VI canonised him in 1977.

StJamesAp.about: James, son of Zebedee and brother of Saint John, was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee when Jesus called him. With Peter and John he was one of the three chosen to witness the raising of Jairus’s daughter, the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane. He is called “the Greater” to distinguish him from the other apostle James. He was the first of the Twelve to die for Christ, put to the sword in Jerusalem by King Herod Agrippa about the year 44, as the Acts of the Apostles records. According to tradition his body rests at Santiago de Compostela in Spain, a great centre of pilgrimage.
StJamesAp.patron: Patron of Spain and of pilgrims

StsJoachimAnne.about: Scripture does not name the parents of the Virgin Mary. The names Joachim and Anne come from an early Christian writing of the second century, the Protoevangelium of James, which tells of an elderly, childless couple whose prayer for a child was answered. Whatever the details, the Church honours the father and mother who brought up Mary and handed on to her the faith of Israel. Devotion to Saint Anne is ancient in the East and spread through the West in the Middle Ages; since 1969 the two have shared this day. Pope Francis placed the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly close to their memorial.

StMartha.about: Martha, Mary and Lazarus were two sisters and a brother who lived at Bethany near Jerusalem and were friends of Jesus, who was welcomed in their home. Saint Luke shows Martha busy with serving while Mary sits at the Lord’s feet and listens. Saint John tells how Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus and raised him from the dead, and how Martha professed her faith in him as the Christ, the Son of God. This day was long kept in honour of Martha alone; in 2021 Pope Francis added her sister and brother, so that the whole household is remembered together.
StMartha.patron: Saint Martha is patron of cooks and of those who serve in the home

StPeterChrysologus.about: Peter was born at Imola in northern Italy and became Bishop of Ravenna, then the residence of the western emperors, about the year 433. He was known for short, clear sermons that explained the Scriptures and the Creed to ordinary people; many of them survive. Their quality later earned him the name Chrysologus, “golden-worded”. When the monk Eutyches, condemned for his teaching about Christ, sought his support, Peter urged him to submit to the judgement of the Pope, Saint Leo the Great. He died at Imola about 450. Benedict XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1729.

StIgnatiusLoyola.about: Ignatius was born in 1491 at Loyola in the Basque country of Spain and lived as a courtier and soldier until a cannonball shattered his leg at Pamplona in 1521. Reading the life of Christ and the lives of the saints during his recovery changed him. He spent months in prayer at Manresa, where the Spiritual Exercises took shape, then studied for years, ending in Paris. There he gathered companions, among them Saint Francis Xavier, who became the Society of Jesus, approved by Pope Paul III in 1540. He governed the Jesuits from Rome until his death in 1556. Their motto is “for the greater glory of God”.

StAlphonsusMariaDeLiguori.about: Alphonsus Liguori was born near Naples in 1696 and was a successful lawyer before he was twenty. Losing an important case showed him the emptiness of worldly success, and he became a priest, preaching simply to the poor of the city and the neglected country people. For them he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, the Redemptorists, in 1732. He later served as Bishop of Sant’Agata dei Goti. His Moral Theology steered between harshness and laxity, and his devotional books, such as The Glories of Mary, are still read. He died in 1787 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1871.
StAlphonsusMariaDeLiguori.patron: Patron of confessors and moral theologians

StEusebius.about: Eusebius was born in Sardinia and served the Church in Rome before becoming the first Bishop of Vercelli in northern Italy about 345. He lived in community with his clergy, sharing prayer and a common rule, the first bishop in the West known to have joined priestly ministry to monastic life in this way. At the Council of Milan in 355 he refused to condemn Saint Athanasius, the great defender of the divinity of Christ against the Arians, and the emperor Constantius banished him to Palestine, Cappadocia and Egypt. Freed after some six years, he returned to rebuild the faith in Italy. He died about 371.

StPeterJulianEymard.about: Peter Julian Eymard was born in 1811 at La Mure in the French Alps. Ordained for the diocese of Grenoble in 1834, he later joined the Marist Fathers and held responsible posts among them. Over the years he became convinced that the Church needed a body of religious devoted wholly to the Eucharist. In 1856 he founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament in Paris, and soon afterwards the Servants of the Blessed Sacrament for women. His priests kept adoration before the Blessed Sacrament and prepared poor adults and children for First Communion. He died at La Mure in 1868 and was canonised by John XXIII in 1962.

StJeanVianney.about: John Mary Vianney was born in 1786 near Lyon, the son of farmers, and grew up during the French Revolution, when priests said Mass in secret. He found study very hard, Latin above all, and was ordained in 1815 chiefly on the strength of his evident goodness. In 1818 he was sent to Ars, a small and indifferent village. By prayer, penance, plain preaching and patient kindness he changed it, and before long people came from all over France to confess to him; in his later years he spent up to sixteen hours a day in the confessional. He died in 1859 and was canonised in 1925.

DedicationStMaryMajor.about: Saint Mary Major stands on the Esquiline Hill in Rome and is one of the oldest churches in the West dedicated to Our Lady. Pope Sixtus III built it soon after the Council of Ephesus in 431 had affirmed that Mary is truly the Mother of God, and its fifth-century mosaics celebrate that faith. A later legend tells that a fall of snow in August marked out the site, which is why the day is also called Our Lady of the Snows.
