The basilica keeps a relic honoured as the crib of Bethlehem and the much-loved icon of Mary known as Salus Populi Romani, protectress of the Roman people.

Transfiguration.about: The Gospels tell how Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, by tradition Mount Tabor in Galilee, and was transfigured before them: his face shone like the sun and his clothes became dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with him, and the Father’s voice came from the cloud, declaring him the beloved Son and commanding the disciples to listen to him. The vision strengthened the apostles for the scandal of the cross and gave a glimpse of the glory of the resurrection. The feast was long kept in the East and was extended to the whole Western Church by Pope Callistus III in 1457.

StCajetan.about: Cajetan was born at Vicenza in 1480 into a noble family, studied law at Padua and worked for a time at the papal court in Rome. Ordained priest in 1516, he gave himself to the care of the sick and incurable and to the renewal of the clergy. In 1524, with Gian Pietro Carafa, later Pope Paul IV, he founded the Clerics Regular, known as the Theatines: priests who lived in community, owned nothing, did not beg, and trusted in God’s providence for their needs. Their example helped to reform the Church from within. He died in Naples in 1547 and was canonised in 1671.
StCajetan.patron: Patron of the unemployed and those seeking work

StSixtusIIPope.about: Sixtus II became Bishop of Rome in 257, during the persecution of the emperor Valerian, whose decrees ordered that bishops, priests and deacons be put to death. On 6 August 258, as he was presiding at a gathering of his people in one of the cemeteries outside the city, soldiers seized him and beheaded him together with four of his deacons. Two more deacons died the same day, and the seventh, Saint Lawrence, four days later. Saint Cyprian of Carthage reported the news in a letter shortly before his own death. Sixtus is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

StDominic.about: Dominic de Guzmán was born about 1170 at Caleruega in Castile and became a canon of the cathedral of Osma. Travelling through southern France, he met the Albigensian heresy, which despised the material world, and saw that it could be answered only by preachers who were both learned and poor. He gathered such men around him, and in 1216 Pope Honorius III approved the Order of Preachers. Dominic sent his friars to the university cities of Europe to study, pray and preach. He died at Bologna in 1221 and was canonised in 1234. Tradition also links him with the spread of the Rosary.

StEdithStein.about: Edith Stein was born in 1891 at Breslau, now Wrocław in Poland, the youngest child of a devout Jewish family. She gave up belief in God as a girl, became a gifted philosopher and worked as assistant to Edmund Husserl. Reading the autobiography of Saint Teresa of Ávila led her to the Catholic faith, and she was baptised in 1922. After years of teaching and writing she entered the Carmel of Cologne in 1933, taking the name Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. Moved to the Netherlands for safety, she was arrested there with her sister Rosa and killed at Auschwitz in August 1942. John Paul II canonised her in 1998.

StLawrenceDeacon.about: Lawrence was one of the seven deacons of Rome under Pope Sixtus II, responsible for the Church’s goods and for the care of the poor. He was put to death on 10 August 258, four days after the Pope, in the persecution of Valerian. According to an early tradition, when the prefect demanded the treasures of the Church, Lawrence gathered the poor, the sick and the widows and presented them as its true wealth, and he was then roasted on a gridiron. He was buried on the Via Tiburtina, where the basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the Walls now stands, and is among Rome’s most loved martyrs.
StLawrenceDeacon.patron: Patron of deacons, cooks and the poor

StClare.about: Clare was born into a noble family of Assisi about 1193. Stirred by the preaching of Saint Francis, she left home in secret on the night of Palm Sunday 1212, and at the little chapel of the Portiuncula Francis cut her hair and clothed her in a rough habit. She settled with her first companions at San Damiano, where she lived enclosed for over forty years as abbess of the community that became the Poor Clares. She held firmly to the privilege of owning nothing, and her Rule, the first written by a woman for religious, was approved by the Pope two days before she died in 1253.

StsPontianHippolytus.about: Pontian became Pope in 230. Hippolytus was a learned Roman priest and one of the foremost theologians of his day, who had quarrelled bitterly with several popes over doctrine and discipline and led a rival group in the city. In 235 the emperor Maximinus sent both men to forced labour in the mines of Sardinia. There Pontian resigned his office so that a successor could be chosen, the first pope known to have done so, and Hippolytus was reconciled to the Church. Both died from the harsh treatment. Their bodies were brought back to Rome and buried on 13 August, and they have been honoured together as martyrs ever since.

StMaximilianKolbe.about: Raymond Kolbe was born in Poland in 1894 and joined the Conventual Franciscans, taking the name Maximilian Mary. As a student in Rome in 1917 he founded the Militia of the Immaculata. He built up a large friary and printing house at Niepokalanów near Warsaw and spent six years as a missionary in Japan. Arrested by the Gestapo in 1941, he was sent to Auschwitz. When ten prisoners were chosen to starve to death, he offered to take the place of a man with a wife and children. He was killed by injection on 14 August 1941. John Paul II canonised him as a martyr in 1982.

Assumption.about: On this day the Church celebrates that Mary, when the course of her earthly life was finished, was taken up body and soul into the glory of heaven. Christians in the East kept the feast as the Dormition, or falling asleep, of the Mother of God from at least the sixth century, and Rome adopted it in the seventh. Pope Pius XII solemnly defined the Assumption as a dogma of faith on 1 November 1950. In Mary the Church sees the first of the redeemed to share fully in her Son’s resurrection, and a sign of sure hope for all who belong to him.

StStephenHungary.about: Stephen was born about 975, son of the Magyar ruler Géza, and was baptised in his youth. He married Gisela, sister of the emperor Saint Henry, and succeeded his father in 997. Around Christmas of the year 1000 he was crowned the first King of Hungary, with a crown that is said to have been sent by Pope Sylvester II. He organised the Church in his kingdom, founding dioceses and monasteries, and drew his people together under Christian law. He is said to have placed the country under the protection of Our Lady. Stephen died on 15 August 1038 and was canonised in 1083.

StJohnEudes.about: John Eudes was born in Normandy in 1601, joined the French Oratory and was ordained priest in 1625. He nursed plague victims and then spent decades preaching parish missions across France. Seeing that the people would be renewed only by better priests, he founded the Congregation of Jesus and Mary, the Eudists, in 1643 to run seminaries. He also founded the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity to shelter women who wanted to leave a life of prostitution. He was a pioneer of liturgical devotion to the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary, composing a Mass and Office in their honour. He died at Caen in 1680.

StBernardClairvaux.about: Bernard was born in 1090 near Dijon in Burgundy. In his early twenties he entered the struggling new monastery of Cîteaux, bringing with him some thirty relatives and friends. In 1115 he was sent to found Clairvaux, which he governed as abbot until his death and from which dozens of further houses sprang. Though he longed for the cloister, he was called on to settle disputes, counsel popes and kings, and preach the Second Crusade. His writings on the love of God, his sermons on the Song of Songs and his devotion to Our Lady have nourished Christians ever since. He died in 1153.

StPiusX.about: Giuseppe Sarto was born in 1835 at Riese in northern Italy, into a family of modest means. He served as curate, parish priest, Bishop of Mantua and Patriarch of Venice before being elected Pope in 1903, and he kept a pastor’s heart throughout. Taking as his motto “to restore all things in Christ”, he encouraged frequent and even daily Communion, admitted children to the sacrament from about the age of seven, promoted catechesis and sacred music, and began the codification of canon law. He firmly opposed the errors of Modernism. He died in August 1914, just as the First World War began, and was canonised in 1954.

QueenshipMary.about: Pope Pius XII established this feast in 1954, during a Marian Year, with the encyclical Ad Caeli Reginam. It was first kept on 31 May; the calendar of 1969 moved it to 22 August, the eighth day after the Assumption, to show that Mary’s queenship follows from her being taken up into glory. Christians have called her Queen for many centuries, as in the Salve Regina and the last mystery of the Rosary. She is Queen because she is Mother of Christ the King and shared most closely in his work of redemption. Her royalty is one of service and intercession.

StRoseLima.about: Isabel Flores de Oliva was born in Lima, Peru, in 1586 and was called Rose from infancy. Taking Saint Catherine of Siena as her model, she became a Dominican tertiary at twenty and lived in a small hut in her parents’ garden, giving herself to prayer and severe penance. She helped to support her family by needlework and growing flowers, and nursed the sick poor in a room of the house. She endured illness, misunderstanding and long periods of spiritual dryness with patience. She died in 1617, aged thirty-one. Canonised in 1671, she was the first person born in the Americas to be declared a saint.
StRoseLima.patron: Patron of Peru, Latin America and the Philippines

StBartholomewAp.about: Bartholomew appears in every list of the twelve apostles in the Gospels and Acts, but nothing more is said of him under that name. He is commonly identified with Nathanael of Cana, whom Philip brought to Jesus and whom the Lord greeted as a true Israelite in whom there was no deceit. Nathanael answered by confessing him as Son of God and King of Israel. According to various traditions Bartholomew preached the Gospel in the East, perhaps as far as India, and was martyred in Armenia, where he is said to have been flayed alive. His relics are venerated at Benevento and in Rome.

StJosephCalasanz.about: Joseph Calasanz was born in Aragon in 1557, was ordained priest in 1583 and came to Rome in 1592. Shocked by the number of poor children growing up without schooling or religious instruction, he opened a free school in the Trastevere district in 1597, often described as the first free public school in Europe. Helpers joined him, and they became the Order of the Pious Schools, the Piarists, who add to the usual vows a promise to educate the young. In old age he was falsely accused and removed from office, which he bore with patience. He died in Rome in 1648, aged about ninety.
StJosephCalasanz.patron: Patron of Christian schools for the people

StLouis.about: Louis IX became King of France in 1226 at the age of twelve, with his mother, Blanche of Castile, ruling as regent. He married Margaret of Provence and they had eleven children. He heard Mass daily, fed the poor at his own table, founded hospitals, and was famed for his fair judgements. He built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to house the relic of the Crown of Thorns. He twice went on crusade: on the first he was taken prisoner in Egypt, and on the second he died of sickness near Tunis in 1270. He was canonised in 1297.
StLouis.patron: Patron of the Secular Franciscan Order

StMonica.about: Monica was born about 332 at Thagaste in North Africa, in what is now Algeria, to a Christian family. She was married to Patricius, a pagan with a quick temper, whom her patience and prayer brought to baptism before his death. Her greatest sorrow was her brilliant son Augustine, who abandoned the faith of his childhood. For many years she prayed and wept for him, and she followed him to Italy. At Milan, under the influence of Saint Ambrose, he was baptised at Easter 387. Monica died at Ostia later that year, on the way home. Augustine tells her story in his Confessions.

StAugustineHippo.about: Augustine was born in 354 at Thagaste in North Africa. A brilliant student and teacher of rhetoric, he spent his youth searching for truth among the Manichees and the philosophers while living as he pleased. The prayers of his mother, Saint Monica, and the preaching of Saint Ambrose in Milan brought him to baptism in 387. Returning to Africa, he was ordained priest and then served as Bishop of Hippo for more than thirty years. His Confessions, The City of God and many other works on grace, the Trinity and the Church have shaped Christian thought ever since. He died in 430 as the Vandals besieged his city.

BeheadingJohnBaptist.about: John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Christ, was imprisoned by Herod Antipas for telling him that it was not lawful to have taken Herodias, his brother’s wife. Saint Mark relates that at a banquet for Herod’s birthday the daughter of Herodias danced, and the king rashly swore to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she demanded John’s head on a dish, and he was beheaded in prison. His disciples took the body and buried it. The Church, which keeps John’s birth in June, has honoured his death on this day since about the fifth century. He died a witness to the truth.

StGregoryGreat.about: Gregory was born about 540 into a senatorial Roman family and rose to be prefect of the city. He gave it up to become a monk, turning his family house on the Caelian Hill into a monastery, and later served as the Pope’s envoy in Constantinople. Elected Pope in 590, in a time of plague, famine and invasion, he fed the people of Rome, negotiated with the Lombards, cared for the liturgy and sent Saint Augustine and his monks to convert the English. He wrote the Pastoral Rule for bishops and called himself “servant of the servants of God”. He died in 604; today marks his consecration as bishop.
StGregoryGreat.patron: Patron of musicians, singers and teachers

StMotherTeresa.about: Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu was born in 1910 in Skopje to an Albanian family. At eighteen she joined the Loreto Sisters and was sent to India, where she taught for nearly twenty years in Calcutta. In 1946, on a train journey, she experienced what she called a call within a call: to leave the convent and serve Christ in the poorest of the poor. She founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1950, caring for the dying, the abandoned and the unwanted, and the congregation spread across the world. She persevered through long years of inner darkness. She died in 1997 and was canonised by Pope Francis in 2016.

NativityVirginMary.about: The Church keeps only three birthdays in her calendar: those of the Lord, of Saint John the Baptist and of Our Lady. Scripture says nothing of Mary’s birth, but Christians have long rejoiced in it as the dawn that announced the coming of Christ, the Sun of justice. The feast began in Jerusalem, probably in the fifth or sixth century, linked with a church built near the Pool of Bethesda at the place held to be the home of her parents, where the church of Saint Anne now stands. It reached Rome in the seventh century. The date falls nine months after the Immaculate Conception on 8 December.

StPeterClaver.about: Peter Claver was born in Catalonia about 1580 and entered the Society of Jesus. Encouraged by the holy doorkeeper Saint Alphonsus Rodriguez, he volunteered for the missions and in 1610 reached Cartagena, in present-day Colombia, a chief slave market of the Spanish Americas. Ordained there in 1616, he later signed his final vows as the slave of the Africans for ever. For some forty years he met the ships as they arrived, going down into the holds with food and medicine, tending the sick, and then instructing and baptising with the help of interpreters. He died in 1654. Leo XIII canonised him in 1888.
StPeterClaver.patron: Patron of missions to African peoples

HolyNameMary.about: As the Church honours the Holy Name of Jesus, so it honours the name of his Mother, which Christians have invoked with trust for many centuries. The feast began in Spain in the sixteenth century. Pope Innocent XI extended it to the whole Church after 12 September 1683, when a Christian army under the Polish king John Sobieski relieved the besieged city of Vienna, a victory attributed to Our Lady’s intercession. Removed from the general calendar in 1969, it was restored by Saint John Paul II in 2002. Saint Luke records simply that the angel was sent to a virgin, “and the virgin’s name was Mary”.

StJohnChrysostom.about: John was born at Antioch in Syria about 349 and trained as an orator before turning to the ascetic life. Ordained priest in 386, he preached for twelve years in Antioch, explaining the Scriptures with a power that later won him the name Chrysostom, “golden mouth”. Made Bishop of Constantinople in 398, he lived simply, cared for the poor, reformed the clergy and spoke plainly against the luxury of the court. His enemies, with the support of the empress Eudoxia, had him deposed and exiled. He died in 407 on a forced march to a more distant place of banishment.

ExaltationCross.about: This feast honours the cross as the instrument of salvation and the sign of Christ’s victory. It goes back to Jerusalem, where the basilica built by the emperor Constantine over Calvary and the tomb of Christ was dedicated on 13 September 335; on the following day the wood of the cross was held up for the people to venerate. According to tradition the cross had been found some years earlier by Constantine’s mother, Saint Helena. The feast also came to recall the recovery of the relic from the Persians by the emperor Heraclius in the seventh century.

OurLadyOfSorrows.about: On the day after the Exaltation of the Cross the Church turns to Mary standing beside it. Simeon had told her in the Temple that a sword would pierce her own soul, and on Calvary she shared her Son’s suffering as no one else could. Devotion to her sorrows, traditionally counted as seven, grew in the Middle Ages and was spread especially by the Servite order. Pope Pius VII extended the feast to the whole Church in 1814, and Saint Pius X fixed it on 15 September. The sequence Stabat Mater may be sung at Mass. Mary stands with all who suffer.

StsCorneliusCyprian.about: Cornelius was elected Pope in 251, after the persecution of Decius had left the Roman see vacant for more than a year. He held, against the rigorist Novatian, that Christians who had denied the faith under threat could be reconciled after penance. Exiled by the emperor Gallus, he died in 253. Cyprian, a convert and gifted orator, became Bishop of Carthage in North Africa about 249. He supported Cornelius and wrote on the unity of the Church. During Valerian’s persecution he was beheaded outside Carthage on 14 September 258. The two friends are named together in the Roman Canon.

StHildegardBingen.about: Hildegard was born in 1098 in the Rhineland and was entrusted as a child to the Benedictine monastery of Disibodenberg, where she later became superior of the nuns. From childhood she experienced visions, which in middle age she felt commanded to write down; Pope Eugene III encouraged the work, known as Scivias. About 1150 she founded a new monastery at Rupertsberg near Bingen. She wrote on theology, medicine and the natural world, composed music still sung today, corresponded with popes and emperors, and preached reform on journeys through Germany. She died in 1179. Benedict XVI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

StRobertBellarmine.about: Robert Bellarmine was born in 1542 at Montepulciano in Tuscany and entered the Society of Jesus in 1560. He taught theology at Louvain and at the Roman College, where his lectures became the Controversies, a thorough answer to the questions raised by the Protestant Reformation. He was spiritual director to Saint Aloysius Gonzaga. Made a cardinal in 1599 and for three years Archbishop of Capua, he lived austerely and gave freely to the poor. His catechisms were used for centuries, and late in life he wrote short works on prayer and on dying well. He died in 1621 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931.

StJanuarius.about: Januarius, in Italian Gennaro, was Bishop of Benevento in southern Italy. According to tradition he was arrested while visiting Christians imprisoned for the faith and was beheaded with several companions near Pozzuoli about the year 305, during the persecution of Diocletian. Little else is known of his life. His relics were eventually brought to Naples, which honours him as its chief patron. In the cathedral there a vial said to contain his blood is shown to the people several times a year, and the dried substance is often seen to become liquid. The Church permits the devotion without having pronounced on its nature.

StAndrewKimTaegon.about: The Church in Korea was begun by lay people, who learned the faith from books brought from China in the late eighteenth century. For decades the community grew with almost no priests and under repeated persecution. This memorial honours 103 martyrs killed in the persecutions of 1839, 1846 and 1866: French missionary bishops and priests and, above all, Korean lay men and women. Andrew Kim Tae-gŏn, the first Korean priest, was ordained in China in 1845 and beheaded near Seoul the following year, aged twenty-five. Paul Chŏng Ha-sang, a lay leader who pleaded for priests to be sent, died in 1839. John Paul II canonised them in Seoul in 1984.

StMatthewEvangelist.about: Matthew was a tax collector at Capernaum, working for the authorities and despised by his neighbours for it. Jesus saw him at his post and said, “Follow me,” and he got up and followed. Mark and Luke call him Levi. He then gave a meal at his house where Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, saying that he had come to call not the righteous but sinners. Matthew was numbered among the Twelve, and from early times the first Gospel has borne his name. Tradition holds that he preached in the East and died a martyr, though accounts of where differ.
StMatthewEvangelist.patron: Patron of bankers, accountants and tax collectors

StPioPietrelcina.about: Francesco Forgione was born in 1887 at Pietrelcina in southern Italy to a farming family. He entered the Capuchins at fifteen, taking the name Pio, and was ordained in 1910. From 1916 he lived at the friary of San Giovanni Rotondo. In 1918 he received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ, in his hands, feet and side, and bore them for fifty years. He spent long hours each day hearing confessions, and people came from all over the world to attend his Mass. Out of concern for the sick he founded a hospital, the House for the Relief of Suffering. He died in 1968 and was canonised in 2002.

StsCosmasDamian.about: Very little is known for certain about Cosmas and Damian beyond the fact that they died for the faith in Syria, probably at Cyrrhus, where a basilica was built over their tomb and where devotion to them was strong by the fifth century. According to tradition they were twin brothers and physicians who treated the sick without taking payment, and were beheaded in the persecution of Diocletian. Their fame spread widely in East and West. In the sixth century Pope Felix IV dedicated a church to them in the Roman Forum, and their names are included in the Roman Canon of the Mass.
StsCosmasDamian.patron: Patrons of physicians, surgeons and pharmacists

StVincentDePaul.about: Vincent de Paul was born in 1581 to a peasant family in Gascony, in south-west France, and was ordained priest in 1600. At first he looked for a comfortable living, but work as a parish priest and as chaplain to a noble household opened his eyes to the poverty and religious neglect of country people. In 1625 he founded the Congregation of the Mission to preach to them and to train the clergy, and in 1633, with Saint Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity to serve the sick and poor. He organised relief for foundlings, galley convicts and war victims. He died in Paris in 1660.
StVincentDePaul.patron: Patron of charitable works and societies

StWenceslaus.about: Wenceslaus was born about 907, son of the Duke of Bohemia, and was brought up in the Christian faith by his grandmother, Saint Ludmila, at a time when much of the country was still pagan. As duke he ruled justly, promoted the Church, built a church in honour of Saint Vitus at Prague Castle and sought peace with his German neighbours. His policies angered some of the nobles, who gathered around his younger brother Boleslaus. Invited by his brother to a feast at Stará Boleslav, Wenceslaus was attacked and killed there on 28 September, probably in 935. He is the patron of the Czech people.

StsLawrenceRuiz.about: This memorial honours sixteen martyrs put to death at Nagasaki in Japan between 1633 and 1637, during a fierce persecution of Christians. Nine were Japanese, four Spanish, one French, one Italian and one Filipino; they included Dominican priests and brothers, lay helpers and two women. Lorenzo Ruiz, born in Manila about 1600 to a Chinese father and a Filipino mother, was a married man with three children who worked as a clerk for the Dominicans. He joined a missionary voyage to Japan in 1636, was arrested, and under torture refused to deny Christ. He died in September 1637. Canonised in 1987, he is the first Filipino saint.

StsArchangels.about: Scripture names three archangels. Michael, whose name means “Who is like God?”, appears in the books of Daniel and Revelation as the leader of the heavenly host and defender of God’s people. Gabriel, “God is my strength”, announced the birth of John the Baptist to Zechariah and of Jesus to Mary. Raphael, “God heals”, is the companion and healer in the Book of Tobit. The date comes from the dedication, long ago, of a basilica of Saint Michael on the Via Salaria near Rome. Since 1969 the three have been honoured together. Angels are God’s messengers and servants, sent to help those who are being saved.

StJerome.about: Jerome was born about 347 at Stridon in Dalmatia and studied in Rome, where he was baptised. After some years as a hermit in the Syrian desert, where he learned Hebrew, he was ordained priest and served as secretary to Pope Damasus, who asked him to revise the Latin text of the Gospels. In 386 he settled in Bethlehem, where he spent over thirty years translating the Old Testament from Hebrew and writing commentaries. His Latin Bible, the Vulgate, served the Western Church for more than a thousand years. Sharp-tongued but wholly devoted to Scripture, he wrote that ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. He died in 420.
StJerome.patron: Patron of biblical scholars, translators and librarians

StThereseChildJesus.about: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in France in 1873 and entered the Carmelite monastery at Lisieux at the age of fifteen. She lived there hidden and unknown, and died of tuberculosis in 1897, aged twenty-four. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, published after her death, made known her “little way”: trusting God as a child trusts a father, and doing small things with great love. She was canonised in 1925, named patron of the missions in 1927 though she never left her convent, and declared a Doctor of the Church by John Paul II in 1997.

GuardianAngels.about: The Church teaches that God gives each person an angel to guard and guide them through life. The belief rests on Scripture: in the Psalms God commands his angels to guard his people, and Jesus says of children that their angels in heaven always behold the face of his Father. A feast in honour of the guardian angels was kept in parts of Spain in the sixteenth century. Pope Paul V placed it in the Roman calendar in 1608, and Clement X later made it binding on the whole Church and fixed it on 2 October. It is a good day to thank God for this unseen care.

StFrancisAssisi.about: Francis was born at Assisi in Italy in 1181 or 1182, the son of a rich cloth merchant. After a carefree youth and a time as a prisoner of war, he gave up his inheritance to live the Gospel in poverty, rebuilding ruined chapels and caring for lepers. Others joined him, and in 1209 Pope Innocent III approved their way of life, the beginning of the Franciscan Order. Francis preached peace, praised God in all creatures, and in 1224 on Mount La Verna received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ, in his body. He died on the evening of 3 October 1226 and was canonised two years later.
StFrancisAssisi.patron: Patron of Italy and of ecology

StFaustinaKowalska.about: Helena Kowalska was born in 1905 into a poor farming family at Głogowiec in Poland. In 1925 she entered the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy in Warsaw, taking the name Maria Faustina, and worked as cook, gardener and doorkeeper. At the request of her confessor she kept a diary recording what she understood Christ to be asking of her: that the world be told of his mercy and learn to trust in it. From this come the image of the Divine Mercy, the chaplet, and Divine Mercy Sunday. She died of tuberculosis in Kraków in 1938 and was canonised by John Paul II in 2000.

StBruno.about: Bruno was born at Cologne about 1030 and for many years was a renowned teacher at the cathedral school of Reims in France. Weary of the corruption he saw among churchmen, he left with six companions in 1084 for a remote Alpine valley near Grenoble called the Chartreuse. There they lived as hermits in community, in silence, prayer and manual work. This was the beginning of the Carthusian Order. Pope Urban II, his former pupil, summoned him to Rome as an adviser, but Bruno soon withdrew again to solitude and founded a second hermitage in Calabria in southern Italy, where he died in 1101.

MarieDurocher.about: Eulalie Durocher was born in 1811 at Saint-Antoine-sur-Richelieu in Quebec. Poor health kept her from entering a convent, and for years she kept house for her brother, a parish priest. There she saw how few schools there were for country children, especially girls. Encouraged by Bishop Ignace Bourget of Montreal, she founded the Sisters of the Holy Names of Jesus and Mary at Longueuil in 1843, taking the name Marie Rose. She died on her thirty-eighth birthday in 1849, worn out by work and illness. The congregation she began spread across Canada and the United States. She was beatified in 1982.

OurLadyOfTheRosary.about: This memorial gives thanks for the help of Mary’s prayers and commends the Rosary, in which the faithful meditate on the life, death and resurrection of Christ while repeating the Hail Mary. It began after 7 October 1571, when a Christian fleet defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto. Pope Pius V, who had asked the faithful to pray the Rosary for the outcome, attributed the victory to Our Lady’s intercession and established a feast of Our Lady of Victory. His successor Gregory XIII renamed it for the Rosary in 1573, and in 1716 Clement XI extended it to the whole Church.

StDenis.about: Denis was the first Bishop of Paris. According to the earliest accounts he was sent from Italy to preach in Gaul about the middle of the third century, and was beheaded for the faith with two companions, traditionally named as the priest Rusticus and the deacon Eleutherius. Tradition places their death on the hill of Montmartre. An abbey grew up over his tomb north of the city, and its church, Saint-Denis, became the burial place of the kings of France. Later legend confused him with Dionysius the Areopagite, who was converted by Saint Paul at Athens.
StDenis.patron: Patron of France and of Paris

StJohnLeonardi.about: John Leonardi was born in 1541 at Diecimo near Lucca in Italy and trained as a pharmacist’s assistant before becoming a priest. He devoted himself to teaching Christian doctrine to the young, and in 1574 gathered a group of priests that became the Clerks Regular of the Mother of God. His zeal for reform made him enemies in Lucca, and he spent much of his later life in Rome, where popes entrusted him with reforming religious houses and where he helped to found a college for training missionary priests. He died in 1609 after tending the sick during an epidemic, and was canonised in 1938.

StJohnNewman.about: John Henry Newman was born in London in 1801 and became an Anglican clergyman and fellow of Oriel College, Oxford. A leader of the Oxford Movement, he was led by his study of the early Church to the conviction that the Catholic Church was the one founded by Christ. He was received into it on 9 October 1845, founded the Oratory at Birmingham, and wrote widely on faith, conscience, education and the development of doctrine. Leo XIII made him a cardinal in 1879. He died in 1890, was canonised in 2019, and was declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Leo XIV in 2025.

StJohnXXIII.about: Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was born in 1881 to a family of farmers at Sotto il Monte near Bergamo in Italy. Ordained in 1904, he served for many years as a papal diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey, Greece and France, and from 1953 as Patriarch of Venice. Elected pope in 1958 at the age of seventy-six, he surprised the world by calling the Second Vatican Council, which he opened on 11 October 1962, the date now kept as his memorial. His encyclical Pacem in Terris appealed for peace among nations. Remembered for his warmth and simplicity, he died in 1963 and was canonised in 2014.

StCallistusIPope.about: Callistus was a slave in Rome who, after a troubled early life that included a sentence to the mines of Sardinia, was freed and put in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way that still bears his name. He became a deacon and counsellor to Pope Zephyrinus and succeeded him as Bishop of Rome about 217. He was fiercely criticised by the priest Hippolytus for readmitting to communion those who had repented of grave sins, a mercy the Church has upheld. He died about 222 and has been honoured as a martyr since the fourth century.

StTeresaJesus.about: Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada was born at Ávila in Spain in 1515 and entered the Carmelite convent there at twenty. After years of half-hearted prayer she experienced a deep conversion and resolved to live the Carmelite rule in its original poverty and solitude. In 1562 she founded the convent of Saint Joseph in Ávila, the first of seventeen, and with Saint John of the Cross extended the reform to the friars. Her books, among them The Way of Perfection and The Interior Castle, are classics on prayer. She died at Alba de Tormes in 1582 and in 1970 became the first woman declared a Doctor of the Church.

StHedwig.about: Hedwig was born about 1174 at Andechs in Bavaria and was married while still a girl to Henry, later Duke of Silesia, with whom she had seven children. Together they founded monasteries and hospitals, among them the Cistercian convent at Trzebnica in what is now Poland. She lived austerely, cared personally for the poor and the sick, and worked for peace among quarrelling princes. After her husband’s death in 1238 she went to live at Trzebnica. Her son Henry was killed fighting the Mongol invaders in 1241. She died in 1243 and was canonised in 1267.

StMargaretAlacoque.about: Margaret Mary Alacoque was born in Burgundy in France in 1647 and in 1671 entered the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial. Between 1673 and 1675 she received a series of visions in which Christ showed her his heart, burning with love for humanity and wounded by indifference. He asked for a feast of the Sacred Heart, for Communion on the first Friday of each month, and for prayer in reparation. She met with disbelief in her community, but was supported by her Jesuit confessor, Saint Claude La Colombière. She died in 1690 and was canonised in 1920. The devotion she promoted spread throughout the Church.

StIgnatiusAntioch.about: Ignatius was Bishop of Antioch in Syria at the beginning of the second century. In the reign of the emperor Trajan he was arrested, condemned to be thrown to wild beasts, and taken under guard to Rome. On the journey he wrote seven letters, which survive, to Christian communities and to Saint Polycarp. They urge unity around the bishop, defend the true humanity of Christ, speak of the Eucharist as the flesh of the Saviour, and contain the earliest known use of the phrase “the Catholic Church”. He begged the Christians of Rome not to prevent his martyrdom, calling himself the wheat of God. He died there about 107.

StLukeEvangelist.about: Luke is the author of the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Saint Paul calls him “the beloved physician”, and passages in Acts written in the first person suggest that he travelled with Paul on some of his journeys and to Rome. Early tradition holds that he was a Gentile from Antioch in Syria. His Gospel alone records the Annunciation, the Magnificat, the shepherds at Bethlehem, and the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, and it shows particular care for the poor, for women and for sinners. A later tradition says that he painted an image of the Virgin Mary.

StPaulCross.about: Paul Danei was born in 1694 at Ovada in northern Italy. As a young man he became convinced that God was calling him to found a community devoted to the memory of the Passion of Christ. He wrote its rule during a forty-day retreat in 1720, and with his brother John Baptist began the first house on Monte Argentario in Tuscany. The Passionists, as they came to be called, combined a life of prayer and penance with preaching missions to the people. Paul was among the most noted preachers of his century and a wise spiritual guide. He died in Rome in 1775 and was canonised in 1867.

StsJeanBrebeuf.about: These eight French missionaries, six Jesuit priests and two lay assistants, gave their lives in the 1640s bringing the Gospel to the native peoples of North America. John de Brébeuf lived among the Hurons in what is now Ontario, learning their language and customs; he and Gabriel Lalemant were killed by Iroquois raiders in 1649. Isaac Jogues, captured and mutilated in 1642, escaped to France and chose to return. He was killed in 1646 at a Mohawk village in what is now New York State, where René Goupil and John de La Lande also died. Antoine Daniel, Charles Garnier and Noël Chabanel complete the group. They were canonised in 1930.

StJohnPaulII.about: Karol Wojtyła was born at Wadowice in Poland in 1920. Under the German occupation he worked in a quarry and a chemical factory while studying secretly for the priesthood, and was ordained in 1946. He became Archbishop of Kraków in 1964 and in 1978 was elected the first non-Italian pope in more than four centuries. Over nearly twenty-seven years he travelled to more than a hundred countries, helped to bring about the peaceful end of communism in Eastern Europe, and taught tirelessly on human dignity, the family and the mercy of God. He died in 2005 and was canonised in 2014. His memorial marks the day his pontificate was inaugurated.

StJohnCapistrano.about: John was born in 1386 at Capestrano in the Abruzzi region of Italy, studied law at Perugia and became governor of that city. Imprisoned during a local war, he reconsidered his life and at about thirty joined the Franciscans, where he was a disciple of Saint Bernardine of Siena. For forty years he preached throughout Italy and central Europe, drawing great crowds, and worked to reform his order. At seventy he helped to rally and lead the Christian army that relieved Belgrade from an Ottoman siege in 1456. He died of illness a few months afterwards and was canonised in 1690.

StAnthonyMaryClaret.about: Anthony Claret was born in 1807 at Sallent in Catalonia, Spain, and worked in the textile trade before becoming a priest in 1835. For years he travelled through Catalonia and the Canary Islands preaching missions and giving retreats, and he wrote and distributed great numbers of religious books and pamphlets. In 1849 he founded the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, the Claretians. Soon afterwards he was sent as Archbishop of Santiago in Cuba, where he reformed the clergy, defended the enslaved and the poor, and survived an attempt on his life. Later confessor to Queen Isabella II, he died in exile in France in 1870.

StSimonStJudeAp.about: Simon and Jude appear in the lists of the twelve apostles in the Gospels. Simon is called “the Zealot”, perhaps because of his zeal for the Jewish Law, and so is distinguished from Simon Peter. Jude, also called Thaddaeus, asks Jesus at the Last Supper why he reveals himself to the disciples and not to the world; the short New Testament Letter of Jude is traditionally attributed to him. Little else is known for certain. According to a Western tradition they preached the Gospel together in Persia and were martyred there. Saint Jude is widely invoked as a helper in desperate situations.
StSimonStJudeAp.patron: Saint Jude is patron of desperate causes

AllSaints.about: On this day the Church honours all the saints in heaven: not only those formally canonised, but the countless men and women of every age who now see God, most of them known to him alone. Feasts of all the martyrs were kept in the East from the fourth century. In Rome, Pope Boniface IV dedicated the Pantheon to Mary and all the martyrs in 609. In the eighth century Gregory III dedicated a chapel in Saint Peter’s to all the saints, and in the following century the feast on 1 November spread throughout the West. It is a reminder that holiness is the calling of every baptised person.

AllSouls.about: On the day after All Saints the Church prays for all who have died in God’s friendship but are still being purified before they see him face to face. Prayer for the dead is found in the Second Book of Maccabees and has been part of Christian worship from the earliest centuries. The custom of a single day for all the departed began with Saint Odilo, Abbot of Cluny, who ordered it for his monasteries about 998; from there it spread across the Western Church. It is a day to pray for the dead, to visit their graves, and to entrust them to the mercy of God.

StMartinPorres.about: Martin was born in Lima in Peru in 1579, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed woman of African descent. He was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon and at fifteen entered the Dominican priory of the Holy Rosary as a lay helper, later becoming a professed brother. There he served for the rest of his life as infirmarian, barber and almoner, nursing the sick of every race and rank, feeding the poor each day, and helping to found a home for orphans and abandoned children. He spent long hours of the night in prayer. He died in 1639 and was canonised by John XXIII in 1962.
StMartinPorres.patron: Patron of social justice and of people of mixed race

StCharlesBorromeo.about: Charles Borromeo was born in 1538 at Arona on Lake Maggiore in northern Italy. His uncle, Pope Pius IV, made him a cardinal at twenty-one and entrusted him with the see of Milan, and he played a leading part in bringing the Council of Trent to its conclusion in 1563. Then, unusually for the time, he went to live in his diocese and set about putting the council into practice: founding seminaries, visiting parishes, holding synods, teaching the catechism to children, and reforming the clergy. During the plague of 1576 he stayed in Milan, feeding and tending the sick. He died in 1584, aged forty-six, and was canonised in 1610.
StCharlesBorromeo.patron: Patron of catechists, seminarians and bishops

DedicationLateran.about: The Lateran Basilica in Rome, not Saint Peter’s, is the cathedral of the Pope as Bishop of Rome. The emperor Constantine gave the Lateran palace to the Church, and the basilica built there was dedicated by Pope Sylvester I about 324. Dedicated to the Most Holy Saviour, it later took the names of the two Saints John, the Baptist and the Evangelist. An inscription on its front calls it the mother and head of all the churches of the city and the world. By keeping the anniversary of its dedication, Catholics everywhere express their unity with the See of Peter and recall that the Church herself is God’s living temple.

StLeoGreat.about: Leo was born towards the end of the fourth century and was a deacon of the Roman Church before being elected pope in 440. He governed for twenty-one years as the Western Empire was collapsing. His letter to Flavian of Constantinople, known as the Tome, set out that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human; the Council of Chalcedon accepted it in 451. In 452 he went out to meet Attila the Hun and persuaded him to withdraw, and in 455 he obtained from the Vandals that Rome should not be burned. He died in 461 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1754.

StMartinTours.about: Martin was born about 316 at Sabaria in Pannonia, now Szombathely in Hungary, the son of a Roman officer, and was enrolled in the army as a youth. While still a catechumen at Amiens he cut his cloak in two to clothe a freezing beggar, and that night saw Christ in a dream wearing the half he had given. After baptism he left the army, became a disciple of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, and founded at Ligugé the first monastery in Gaul. Made Bishop of Tours about 371 against his will, he continued to live as a monk and travelled the countryside preaching to pagans. He died in 397.

StJosaphat.about: John Kuntsevych was born about 1580 at Volodymyr in what is now Ukraine, into an Orthodox family. As a young man he embraced the Union of Brest of 1596, by which part of the Ruthenian Church entered into communion with Rome while keeping its Eastern liturgy. He became a Basilian monk at Vilnius, taking the name Josaphat, and in 1618 became Archbishop of Polotsk. He worked tirelessly by preaching, example and reform of the clergy to win people to unity, and met fierce opposition. On 12 November 1623 a mob at Vitebsk, in present-day Belarus, attacked his residence and killed him. He was canonised in 1867.

StFrancesXCabrini.about: Frances Cabrini was born in 1850 at Sant’Angelo Lodigiano in Lombardy. Refused by two convents because of poor health, she founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in 1880. She hoped to go to China, but Pope Leo XIII directed her instead to the Italian emigrants in America, and she arrived in New York in 1889. Over twenty-eight years she crossed the ocean many times and founded 67 schools, hospitals and orphanages in the United States, Latin America and Europe. She became an American citizen in 1909, died in Chicago in 1917, and in 1946 became the first citizen of the United States to be canonised.

StAlbertGreat.about: Albert was born about 1200 at Lauingen on the Danube in Germany and joined the Dominicans as a student at Padua. He taught at Paris and Cologne, where Thomas Aquinas was his pupil, and wrote on almost every branch of learning then known, from theology to botany, astronomy and minerals. He showed that the philosophy of Aristotle and the careful study of nature could serve the Christian faith rather than threaten it. He served as Dominican provincial and for a short time as Bishop of Regensburg, then returned to teaching. He died at Cologne in 1280, and in 1931 was canonised and declared a Doctor of the Church.

StGertrudeGreat.about: Gertrude was born in 1256 and from the age of five was brought up in the monastery of Helfta in Saxony, Germany, a house noted for its learning. She was a gifted student, devoted to literature. At twenty-five she had a vision of Christ that turned her wholly towards prayer and the study of Scripture and the Fathers of the Church. Her writings, chiefly The Herald of Divine Love and her Spiritual Exercises, are rooted in the liturgy and speak of her intimate friendship with Christ and her trust in his heart, long before devotion to the Sacred Heart became widespread. She died at Helfta about 1302.

StMargaretScotland.about: Margaret was born about 1045 in Hungary, where her father, an English prince, was living in exile. The family returned to England, but after the Norman Conquest of 1066 fled north, and about 1070 Margaret married Malcolm III, King of Scots. As queen she fed the poor and orphans with her own hands, encouraged the reform of the Church in Scotland, founded the abbey of Dunfermline, and provided a ferry for pilgrims travelling to Saint Andrews. She raised eight children, three of whom became kings. She died at Edinburgh Castle in 1093, a few days after her husband and eldest son were killed in battle, and was canonised in 1250.

StElizabethHungary.about: Elizabeth was born in 1207, daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary, and was sent as a child to the court of Thuringia in Germany, where at fourteen she married the landgrave Louis IV. The marriage was happy, and they had three children. Influenced by the first Franciscans, she used her position to feed the hungry and nurse the sick. When Louis died on his way to the crusade in 1227, she left the court, took the habit of a Franciscan penitent, and built a hospital at Marburg where she served the poorest with her own hands. She died there in 1231, aged twenty-four, and was canonised in 1235.
StElizabethHungary.patron: Patron of the Secular Franciscan Order and of charitable works

DedicationStsPeterPaul.about: This day recalls the dedication of the two Roman basilicas built over the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul. The first churches on these sites were begun in the fourth century under the emperor Constantine: Saint Peter’s on the Vatican hill, and Saint Paul’s on the road to Ostia, outside the city walls. The present Saint Peter’s was consecrated by Pope Urban VIII on 18 November 1626. Saint Paul’s was largely destroyed by fire in 1823, rebuilt, and consecrated by Pius IX in 1854. Pilgrims have prayed at these tombs since the earliest centuries. The memorial honours the two apostles together as the founders of the Church in Rome.

StRoseDuchesne.about: Rose Philippine Duchesne was born at Grenoble in France in 1769. She entered the Visitation order, but the French Revolution closed her convent, and in 1804 she joined the newly founded Society of the Sacred Heart under Saint Madeleine Sophie Barat. In 1818, aged forty-eight, she sailed with four companions for the Mississippi valley and opened at Saint Charles, Missouri, the first free school west of the river. More schools and convents followed. At seventy-one she fulfilled her wish to live among Native Americans, spending a year with the Potawatomi in Kansas, who named her the woman who prays always. She died in 1852 and was canonised in 1988.

PresentationMary.about: This memorial celebrates Mary’s dedication to God from her earliest years. It draws on an ancient tradition, found not in Scripture but in the second-century writing known as the Protoevangelium of James, that her parents Joachim and Anne brought her as a child to the Temple in Jerusalem and offered her to the Lord. The feast began in the East, linked to the dedication of a church of Saint Mary in Jerusalem in 543. It was adopted by the papal court at Avignon in 1372 and, after being dropped for a time, was restored to the Roman calendar in 1585. Its meaning is that Mary belonged wholly to God, who prepared her to become the dwelling place of his Son.

StCecilia.about: Cecilia is one of the most honoured of the Roman martyrs, named in the Roman Canon, though little is known of her with certainty. A church in Trastevere in Rome has borne her name since at least the fifth century. According to the account of her martyrdom, written long afterwards, she was a young Christian noblewoman who had vowed her virginity to God, won her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to the faith, and was put to death after them. Because the account says that she sang to the Lord in her heart on her wedding day, she came to be regarded as the patron of music.
StCecilia.patron: Patron of musicians and church music

StClementIPope.about: Clement was Bishop of Rome at the end of the first century, the third successor of Saint Peter according to Saint Irenaeus. He is known above all for a letter sent from the Church of Rome about the year 96 to the Church of Corinth, where some members had deposed their presbyters. The letter calls for humility, peace and respect for those appointed in succession from the apostles, and is one of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament. A later tradition, which cannot be verified, says that he was exiled to the Crimea under the emperor Trajan and drowned with an anchor tied to his neck.

StColumban.about: Columban was born in Leinster in Ireland about 543 and became a monk at Bangor under Saint Comgall. About 590 he set out with twelve companions for the continent as a pilgrim for Christ. In the Vosges mountains of eastern France he founded monasteries at Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaines, which followed his austere rule and drew many vocations. His outspoken rebuke of the Burgundian king’s immoral life led to his expulsion. He travelled on through what are now Switzerland and Austria and into Italy, where about 614 he founded the abbey of Bobbio. He died there in 615. His monks helped to renew Christian life and learning across Europe.

MiguelPro.about: Miguel Pro was born in 1891 at Guadalupe in the Mexican state of Zacatecas and entered the Jesuits at twenty. Driven abroad by the revolution, he studied in Spain and Belgium, where he was ordained in 1925. He returned to Mexico in 1926, as the government of President Calles suppressed public worship. For over a year he ministered in secret in Mexico City, often in disguise, bringing the sacraments and relief to the poor. Falsely accused of plotting to kill a former president, he was shot without trial on 23 November 1927. He died with arms outstretched like a cross, proclaiming Christ the King. He was beatified in 1988.

StAndrewDungLac.about: The Gospel reached Vietnam in the sixteenth century, and over the following three hundred years Christians there suffered repeated persecution in which very many died. This memorial honours 117 of them, martyred between 1745 and 1862 and canonised together by John Paul II in 1988. Ninety-six were Vietnamese and the rest missionaries from Spain and France. They include eight bishops, fifty priests and fifty-nine lay people. Andrew Dũng-Lạc, who heads the list, was a Vietnamese diocesan priest beheaded in Hanoi in 1839. Among the others are the French missionary priest Théophane Vénard and Agnes Lê Thị Thành, a mother of six who died in prison.

StCatherineAlexandria.about: Catherine is venerated as a virgin martyr of Alexandria, said to have been put to death in the early fourth century. Nothing certain is known of her life. According to her legend, she was a learned noblewoman who rebuked the emperor for persecuting Christians, overcame in debate the philosophers he sent to refute her, and was condemned to die on a spiked wheel; when the wheel broke, she was beheaded. Her body is said to have been carried to Mount Sinai, where the ancient monastery bears her name. She was among the most popular saints of the Middle Ages. Her memorial was restored to the general calendar in 2002.

StAndrewAp.about: Andrew was a fisherman from Bethsaida in Galilee and the brother of Simon Peter. According to Saint John’s Gospel he was first a disciple of John the Baptist, was one of the first two to follow Jesus, and at once brought his brother to him; for this the Eastern Churches call him the “first-called”. It is Andrew who points out the boy with the loaves and fishes, and who with Philip tells Jesus that some Greeks wish to see him. According to tradition he preached in Greece and was crucified at Patras on an X-shaped cross. The Church of Constantinople honours him as its founder.
StAndrewAp.patron: Patron of fishermen, and of Scotland, Greece and Russia

StFrancisXavier.about: Francis was born in 1506 at the castle of Xavier in Navarre, Spain. As a student in Paris he met Ignatius of Loyola, and in 1534 he was one of the first seven companions who took vows at Montmartre, the beginning of the Society of Jesus. Sent to the East, he reached Goa in India in 1542 and spent ten years preaching in southern India, Malacca, the Moluccas and Japan, where he landed in 1549. He baptised many thousands and organised the communities he left behind. He died of fever on the island of Shangchuan in December 1552, waiting to enter China. He was canonised in 1622.

StJohnDamascene.about: John was born about 675 into a Christian family of Damascus in Syria, then the capital of the Muslim caliphate. He became a monk and priest at the monastery of Saint Sabas near Jerusalem. When the Byzantine emperor forbade the veneration of sacred images, John wrote three treatises in their defence: because the Son of God truly became man and visible, he can be depicted, and the honour paid to an image passes to the one it represents. His great work, The Fount of Knowledge, gathered up the teaching of the Greek Fathers. He died about 749 and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1890.

StNicholas.about: Nicholas was Bishop of Myra in Lycia, in what is now southern Turkey, in the fourth century. Almost nothing certain is known of his life, but he was honoured early in the East as a pastor of great charity and a worker of miracles. The best-known story tells that he secretly threw bags of gold through the window of a poor man’s house to provide dowries for his three daughters. In 1087 his relics were carried by sailors to Bari in southern Italy, where they remain. His reputation for giving in secret lies behind the figure of Santa Claus. He is venerated by Christians of East and West alike.

StAmbrose.about: Ambrose was born about 340 at Trier in Germany and became governor of the province centred on Milan. In 374, while he was trying to keep the peace at the election of a new bishop, the people called for him to be bishop himself, though he was not yet baptised. He was baptised and then ordained bishop on 7 December. He gave his wealth to the poor, studied Scripture intensely, resisted the Arian heresy, and did not hesitate to call the emperor Theodosius to public penance after a massacre at Thessalonica. His preaching helped to convert Saint Augustine, whom he baptised in 387. He died in 397.
StAmbrose.patron: Patron of Milan and of beekeepers

ImmaculateConception.about: This solemnity celebrates the truth that Mary, from the first moment of her conception, was preserved by God from all stain of original sin, in view of the merits of her Son. It does not refer to the conception of Jesus. A feast of Mary’s conception was kept in the East from the seventh or eighth century and spread through the West in the Middle Ages. Pope Pius IX defined the doctrine in 1854. Four years later at Lourdes, the Lady who appeared to Bernadette named herself the Immaculate Conception. Under this title Mary is patroness of the United States, where the day is a holy day of obligation.

JuanDiego.about: Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin was born about 1474 near what is now Mexico City. He and his wife were among the first of the indigenous people there to be baptised after the arrival of the Franciscan missionaries. In December 1531, the Virgin Mary appeared to him on the hill of Tepeyac and sent him to ask the bishop to build a church there. As a sign she had him gather roses in his cloak, and when he opened it before the bishop her image was seen upon it. He spent his remaining years as a hermit beside the chapel built there, and died in 1548. He was canonised in 2002.

OurLadyOfLoreto.about: The shrine of Loreto, near the Adriatic coast of Italy, has drawn pilgrims since the Middle Ages. Within its basilica stands the Holy House, three stone walls venerated as part of the house at Nazareth where Mary received the angel’s message and where the Holy Family lived. According to tradition the house was brought from the Holy Land at the end of the thirteenth century, when the crusaders were driven out; legend says that angels carried it. For this reason Our Lady of Loreto was named patron of aviators in 1920. Pope Francis placed this memorial in the general calendar in 2019, to honour the mystery of the Incarnation.
OurLadyOfLoreto.patron: Patron of aviators and air travellers

StDamasusIPope.about: Damasus was born about 305, probably in Rome, where his father served the church of Saint Lawrence. Elected pope in 366 amid violent disputes with a rival, he governed for eighteen years as Christianity became the religion of the empire. He upheld the faith of Nicaea against Arianism and other errors, and affirmed the authority of the Roman See as founded on Saint Peter. He asked his secretary, Saint Jerome, to revise the Latin text of the Scriptures, the beginning of the Vulgate. He also restored the tombs of the Roman martyrs and composed verse inscriptions in their honour, some of which survive. He died in 384.

OurLadyOfGuadalupe.about: Between 9 and 12 December 1531, ten years after the Spanish conquest of Mexico, the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego, an indigenous convert, on the hill of Tepeyac outside Mexico City. Speaking in his own Nahuatl language, she asked for a church to be built there and told him not to be afraid, for she was his mother. Her image, showing her as a young woman of the country, was left on his cloak, which is still venerated in the basilica on the site. In the years that followed, great numbers of the native peoples accepted the faith. Her shrine is among the most visited in the world.

StJaneFrancesDeChantal.about: Jane Frances Frémyot was born at Dijon in France in 1572 and at twenty married the Baron de Chantal, with whom she had six children. Her husband was killed in a hunting accident in 1601, and she struggled for a long time to forgive the man responsible. In 1604 she met Saint Francis de Sales, who became her spiritual guide and friend. With him she founded the Order of the Visitation at Annecy in 1610, open to women whose age or health barred them from stricter orders. By her death at Moulins in 1641 there were more than eighty houses. She was canonised in 1767.

StLucySyracuse.about: Lucy was martyred at Syracuse in Sicily, most probably about 304 during the persecution of Diocletian. She was venerated there from an early date, and she is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass. The later account of her death says that she had consecrated her virginity to Christ and given her dowry to the poor, and that a rejected suitor denounced her as a Christian. Her name comes from the Latin word for light, and her feast, falling in the darkest days of the year, is kept with festivals of light, especially in Scandinavia. She is invoked by those who suffer from diseases of the eyes.
StLucySyracuse.patron: Patron of the blind and of those with eye disease

StJohnCross.about: Juan de Yepes was born in 1542 at Fontiveros in Spain. He became a Carmelite friar and was ordained in 1567, the year he met Saint Teresa of Ávila, who persuaded him to join her reform. In 1568 he helped to begin the first house of Discalced Carmelite friars at Duruelo. Friars opposed to the reform imprisoned him in Toledo for almost nine months, and there he began to compose his finest poetry. His works, among them The Dark Night and The Spiritual Canticle, trace the soul’s journey to union with God. He died at Úbeda in 1591 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926.

StPeterCanisius.about: Peter Kanis was born in 1521 at Nijmegen in the Netherlands and in 1543 became the first Dutchman to join the Jesuits. For half a century he laboured to renew Catholic life in the German-speaking lands in the wake of the Reformation: preaching, teaching in universities, advising bishops and princes, taking part in the Council of Trent, and founding colleges from Prague to Fribourg. His three catechisms, written for different ages, went through hundreds of editions. He was known for arguing with courtesy rather than abuse. He died at Fribourg in Switzerland in 1597, and in 1925 was canonised and declared a Doctor of the Church.

StJohnKanty.about: John was born in 1390 at Kęty, a town near Kraków in Poland, and spent almost all his life at the university of Kraków as a student, priest and professor, first of philosophy and then of theology. For a short time he was removed from his chair and sent to be a parish priest, a charge he carried out faithfully before being recalled. He was loved for his learning, his humility and above all his generosity: he lived on very little and gave the rest of his income, and often his own food and clothing, to the poor. He died in 1473 and was canonised in 1767.

StStephenProtomartyr.about: Stephen, as the Acts of the Apostles relates, was one of the seven men whom the apostles chose in Jerusalem to care for the daily distribution to widows; the Church regards them as the first deacons. He preached with power and was accused before the Sanhedrin of speaking against the Temple and the Law. After a long speech recalling Israel’s history, he declared that he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man at God’s right hand. He was dragged out of the city and stoned, praying that his killers be forgiven, while a young man named Saul looked on with approval. He is the first Christian martyr.

StJohnEvangelist.about: John, the son of Zebedee and brother of James, was a Galilean fisherman. With Peter and James he witnessed the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane. Tradition identifies him with the “disciple whom Jesus loved”, who reclined beside the Lord at the Last Supper, stood by the cross, received Mary into his care, and ran to the empty tomb. The fourth Gospel, three letters and the Book of Revelation bear his name. According to early tradition he lived to old age at Ephesus, the only apostle not to die a martyr. His symbol is the eagle, for the height of his teaching on the Word made flesh.

HolyInnocents.about: Saint Matthew’s Gospel tells that King Herod, hearing from the wise men of the birth of a king of the Jews and fearing for his throne, ordered the killing of all boys aged two and under in Bethlehem and its neighbourhood. Joseph, warned in a dream, had already taken the child and his mother to Egypt. The Church has honoured these children as martyrs since at least the fifth century: they died not knowing Christ, yet in his place. Their feast within the Christmas octave sets the joy of the Nativity beside the suffering of the innocent, and is a fitting day to pray for all children in danger.

StThomasBecket.about: Thomas Becket was born in London about 1120. Able and ambitious, he rose to be chancellor of England and close friend of King Henry II, who in 1162 had him made Archbishop of Canterbury, expecting a compliant ally. Instead Thomas changed his way of life and firmly resisted the king’s attempts to bring the Church and its courts under royal control. He spent six years in exile in France. Within weeks of his return, on 29 December 1170, four knights who had heard the king’s angry words killed him in his cathedral. He was canonised in 1173, and Canterbury became one of the great pilgrim shrines of Europe.

StSylvesterIPope.about: Sylvester, a Roman, was pope from 314 to 335, the years immediately after the emperor Constantine ended the persecution of Christians. Little is recorded of his own actions, but his pontificate saw the Church emerge into public life. The Roman basilicas were begun in his time, among them the Lateran and the first Saint Peter’s. He did not attend the Council of Nicaea in 325, which defined that the Son is of one substance with the Father, but sent two priests to represent him. Later legends, such as that he baptised Constantine, are not historical. He died on 31 December 335 and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla.

BlFrancisXavierSeelos.about: Francis Xavier Seelos was born in Bavaria and came to the United States in 1843 to join the Redemptorists and serve German-speaking immigrants. He was ordained in Baltimore and worked for nine years in Pittsburgh, at first under Saint John Neumann, whom he succeeded as pastor. Patient and cheerful, he was sought out as a confessor by people of every background, and later preached parish missions across a dozen states. Sent to New Orleans in 1866, he caught yellow fever while visiting the sick and died the following year. He was beatified in 2000.

advent.about: Advent opens the Church’s year. It begins on the Sunday falling on or nearest to 30 November and runs through four Sundays to the evening of 24 December. The season has a double meaning: it prepares for Christmas, when the first coming of the Son of God is remembered, and it turns minds towards his coming again at the end of time. The colour is violet, the Gloria is left out at Sunday Mass, and the readings, many of them from Isaiah and about John the Baptist, are full of quiet, expectant hope. A simple way to keep it is to light the candles of an Advent wreath at home each evening and pray together for a few minutes.

christmas.about: The Christmas season celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ and the first signs by which he was made known to the world. It runs from the evening of 24 December to the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, and includes the eight days of the Christmas octave, the feast of the Holy Family, the solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, and the Epiphany. The colour is white, the Gloria returns, and the spirit is one of joy and wonder that God has become man. Since the season lasts well beyond 25 December, a good way to keep it is to leave the crib in place at home and pray before it each day until the season ends.

ordinary.about: Ordinary Time is the name for the thirty-three or thirty-four weeks of the year that fall outside the great seasons. It comes in two stretches: a shorter one between the Baptism of the Lord and Ash Wednesday, and a longer one from the Monday after Pentecost until Advent. No single mystery is singled out. Instead the Church follows the life and teaching of Christ week by week, reading mainly from one of the Gospels of Matthew, Mark or Luke over the Sundays of each year. The colour is green, a sign of growth and hope. A good way to keep it is to read the coming Sunday’s Gospel slowly at home beforehand.

lent.about: Lent is the season of about forty days that prepares for Easter, running from Ash Wednesday to the evening of Holy Thursday. It recalls the forty days Jesus fasted in the desert. The Church asks for prayer, fasting and almsgiving, while those to be baptised at Easter make their final preparation. The colour is violet, the Alleluia is not sung, and the Gloria is left out on Sundays. Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and abstinence, and the Fridays of Lent are days of penance, kept in most countries by abstaining from meat. A good practice is to go to confession and to give to the poor what is saved by fasting.

holy-week.about: Holy Week is the last week before Easter, from Palm Sunday to Holy Saturday. In it the Church follows Jesus step by step through his final days: the entry into Jerusalem, the Last Supper, his arrest, trial, death and burial. Lent continues until Thursday evening, when the Paschal Triduum begins. The colours change with the days: red on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, violet on the weekdays, white on Holy Thursday. The spirit is one of close and sober attention to the Passion. The best way to keep the week is to take part in the liturgies themselves, and at home to read one of the Gospel accounts of the Passion through from beginning to end.

triduum.about: The Paschal Triduum is the three days at the centre of the whole Christian year. It begins with the evening Mass of the Lord’s Supper on Holy Thursday, continues through the Celebration of the Lord’s Passion on Good Friday and the silence of Holy Saturday, reaches its height in the Easter Vigil, and closes with Evening Prayer on Easter Sunday. The Church treats these days as a single celebration of the death and resurrection of Christ. The colour is white on Thursday, red on Friday and white at the Vigil. The best way to keep these days is to arrange work and family life so as to attend all three liturgies.

easter.about: The Easter season is fifty days of rejoicing in the resurrection of Christ, from Easter Sunday to Pentecost. The Church keeps the whole of it as one feast day, sometimes called the “great Sunday”. The colour is white, the Alleluia returns and is sung often, the Paschal candle burns in the sanctuary, and the first reading at Mass is taken from the Acts of the Apostles in place of the Old Testament. The first eight days form the Easter octave. The season includes the Ascension and ends with the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. One way to keep it is to pray the Regina Caeli in place of the Angelus each day.

Christmas.about: The Nativity of the Lord, 25 December, celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ at Bethlehem, told in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, and the truth proclaimed at the opening of John’s Gospel that the Word became flesh. The feast is recorded at Rome on this date by the middle of the fourth century. The Missal gives four Masses, each with its own readings: the Vigil on the evening before, the Mass during the Night, the Mass at Dawn and the Mass during the Day. In the Creed all genuflect at the words that speak of the Incarnation, as on the Annunciation; otherwise they bow. The colour is white.

HolyFamily.about: The feast of the Holy Family of Jesus, Mary and Joseph is kept on the Sunday within the octave of Christmas, or on 30 December when Christmas falls on a Sunday. It honours the hidden years at Nazareth, where the Son of God grew up in an ordinary home. The Gospel is taken from the accounts of his childhood: the flight into Egypt, the presentation in the Temple, or the finding of the boy Jesus among the teachers. Pope Benedict XV placed the feast in the calendar of the whole Church in 1921. It is a good day to pray for one’s own family.

MaryMotherOfGod.about: On 1 January, the eighth day of Christmas, the Church keeps the solemnity of Mary, the Holy Mother of God. The title, in Greek Theotokos, was upheld by the Council of Ephesus in 431: because Jesus is one person, truly God and truly man, his mother is rightly called Mother of God. The Gospel tells of the shepherds finding the child, of Mary keeping these things in her heart, and of his naming on the eighth day. The solemnity took its present form in the calendar reform of 1969. Whether it is a holy day of obligation varies from country to country.

Epiphany.about: The Epiphany celebrates the showing of Christ to the nations, in the wise men from the east who followed a star to Bethlehem, worshipped the child and offered him gold, frankincense and myrrh, as told in Matthew 2. The feast began in the Christian East and was kept in the West by the fourth century. Its traditional date is 6 January, but in many countries, where it is not a holy day of obligation, it is moved to the Sunday between 2 and 8 January. After the Gospel the dates of Easter and the other movable feasts of the coming year may be announced.

BaptismLord.about: The feast of the Baptism of the Lord recalls Jesus coming to John at the Jordan to be baptised, when the Spirit came down on him like a dove and the Father’s voice declared him his beloved Son. Jesus had no sin to wash away, but he took his place among sinners and so began his public ministry. The feast is normally kept on the Sunday after 6 January, though where the Epiphany is moved to a Sunday falling on 7 or 8 January it is kept on the Monday that follows. It brings the Christmas season to an end, and Ordinary Time begins the next day.

AshWednesday.about: Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent. After the homily, ashes made by burning palms from the previous Palm Sunday are blessed and placed on each person’s head, with the words “Repent, and believe in the Gospel” or “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Ashes are a biblical sign of repentance, in general use in the West at the start of Lent since the eleventh century. The Gospel, from Matthew 6, is the teaching of Jesus on almsgiving, prayer and fasting done in secret. It is a day of fasting and abstinence from meat, but not a holy day of obligation.

PalmSun.about: Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord begins Holy Week. Mass opens with the blessing of palm or other branches and, where possible, a procession into the church, recalling the crowds who welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem crying “Hosanna”. A procession of this kind in Jerusalem was described by the pilgrim Egeria in the late fourth century. The mood then changes. The Gospel is the account of the Passion, from Matthew, Mark or Luke according to the year, and all kneel briefly in silence at the death of the Lord. The vestments are red. The blessed palms are taken home and kept.

HolyThurs.about: On the evening of Holy Thursday the Mass of the Lord’s Supper opens the Paschal Triduum. It commemorates the Last Supper, at which Jesus gave the Eucharist and the priesthood and commanded his disciples to love one another. The Gospel is from John 13, where he washes their feet, and after the homily the priest may wash the feet of some of the faithful. The Gloria is sung with bells, which then stay silent until the Easter Vigil. After Communion the Blessed Sacrament is carried in procession to a place of repose, and the altar is stripped. There is no dismissal. The colour is white.

GoodFri.about: Good Friday commemorates the Passion and death of Jesus on the Cross. No Mass is celebrated. Instead, usually at about three in the afternoon, the Church holds the Celebration of the Passion of the Lord in three parts: the Liturgy of the Word, with the Passion according to John and ten solemn intercessions for the Church and the world; the Adoration of the Holy Cross, when each person comes forward to venerate it; and Holy Communion from hosts consecrated the evening before. The service begins and ends in silence. The vestments are red. It is a day of fasting and abstinence from meat.

EasterVigil.about: On Holy Saturday the Church waits at the Lord’s tomb, meditating on his death and his descent to the dead. The altar is bare, no Mass is celebrated during the day, and Holy Communion is given only to the dying. After nightfall comes the Easter Vigil. A fire is blessed and the Paschal candle is lit from it and carried into the dark church. The Exsultet is sung, and a long series of readings traces the history of salvation from creation to the empty tomb. The Gloria and Alleluia return, new Christians are baptised, and all renew their baptismal promises. The colour is white.

Easter.about: Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead on the third day, the greatest feast of the year. The Gospel, from John 20, tells of Mary Magdalene finding the stone moved away and of Peter and the other disciple running to the empty tomb. The sequence Victimae paschali laudes is sung before the Alleluia. Following the rule associated with the Council of Nicaea in 325, Easter falls on the Sunday after the first full moon of spring as the Church reckons it, so its date moves between 22 March and 25 April.
