The colour is white.

DivineMercySunday.about: The Second Sunday of Easter closes the Easter octave. Its Gospel, from John 20, is the same every year. The risen Jesus appears to the disciples on the evening of Easter and gives them the power to forgive sins, and a week later he invites Thomas to touch his wounds, drawing from him the words “My Lord and my God.” In 2000, at the canonisation of Saint Faustina Kowalska, the Polish nun whose diary spread devotion to the mercy of Christ, Pope John Paul II gave the day the added name of Divine Mercy Sunday. Many parishes hold afternoon devotions with the Chaplet of Divine Mercy.

Ascension.about: The Ascension celebrates the risen Jesus being taken up into heaven in the sight of his apostles, forty days after Easter, as told in Acts 1 and at the end of Luke’s Gospel. He takes his place at the Father’s right hand in his human nature, opening the way for those who belong to him, and promises to send the Holy Spirit. The feast is attested from the fourth century. Its proper day is the Thursday of the sixth week of Easter, but in many countries and dioceses it is moved to the following Sunday, so the date depends on where one lives.

Pentecost.about: Pentecost, fifty days after Easter, celebrates the coming of the Holy Spirit on the disciples gathered in Jerusalem, as told in Acts 2: a sound like a rushing wind, tongues as of fire, and the apostles preaching to people of every language. It took place on the Jewish feast of Weeks, and it is often called the birthday of the Church. The vestments are red, and the sequence Veni Sancte Spiritus is sung before the Gospel. A longer vigil Mass may be celebrated the evening before. Pentecost ends the Easter season. Afterwards the Paschal candle is moved to the baptismal font and Ordinary Time resumes.

Trinity.about: The solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity, on the Sunday after Pentecost, honours the central mystery of the faith: one God in three Persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It is unusual among feasts in celebrating not an event but a truth about God himself, revealed by Christ, who sent his disciples to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). An office of the Trinity was in use in parts of Europe from the tenth century, and Pope John XXII extended the feast to the whole Western Church in the fourteenth. The colour is white.

CorpusChristi.about: The solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, known as Corpus Christi, honours the real presence of Jesus in the Eucharist. It grew from the devotion of Saint Juliana of Liège in the thirteenth century, and Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole Church in 1264. According to tradition Saint Thomas Aquinas composed its prayers and hymns, among them the sequence Lauda Sion and the hymn Pange lingua. Its proper day is the Thursday after Trinity Sunday, but in many countries it is kept on the following Sunday. Mass is often followed by a procession with the Blessed Sacrament through the streets.

SacredHeart.about: The solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus is kept on the Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost. It honours the love of Christ for mankind under the sign of his human heart, pierced by the soldier’s lance on the Cross (John 19:34). The devotion is found among medieval saints and spread widely after the visions of Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque, a Visitation nun at Paray-le-Monial in France, in the 1670s. Pope Pius IX extended the feast to the whole Church in 1856. Practices linked with it are Communion on the first Friday of each month and prayer in reparation for sin.

ImmaculateHeart.about: The memorial of the Immaculate Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary falls on the Saturday after the solemnity of the Sacred Heart. It honours Mary’s interior life: her faith, her purity, and her love for God and for all people. Its root in Scripture is Luke’s remark that Mary “kept all these things in her heart”, and the Gospel of the day is the finding of Jesus in the Temple, where those words occur. Saint John Eudes promoted the devotion in the seventeenth century, and it grew further after the apparitions at Fatima in 1917. Pope Pius XII extended the feast to the whole Church in 1944.

MaryMotherChurch.about: The memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church, is kept on the Monday after Pentecost. Pope Francis added it to the general calendar in 2018. The title itself is older: Pope Paul VI proclaimed Mary Mother of the Church in 1964, during the Second Vatican Council. The Gospel is from John 19, where Jesus on the Cross says to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son,” and to the beloved disciple, “Behold, your mother.” The first reading may be from Acts 1, which shows Mary praying with the apostles as they wait for the Holy Spirit, and this explains the choice of day.

ChristKing.about: The solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe, falls on the last Sunday of the Church’s year. Pope Pius XI established it in 1925 with the encyclical Quas primas, in answer to the growing exclusion of God from public life. In 1969 it was moved from late October to the Sunday before Advent, where it points to the return of Christ in glory. The Gospels show what kind of king he is: the judge who identifies himself with the hungry and the stranger, the prisoner before Pilate whose kingdom is not of this world, the crucified Lord who promises paradise to the repentant thief.

ThanksgivingDay.about: Thanksgiving Day is a civil holiday of the United States, kept on the fourth Thursday of November. It is not a feast of the universal Church and it is not a holy day of obligation, but the Missal used in the United States provides a Mass of thanksgiving for the day, and many Catholics begin the holiday by attending it. A Gospel often read is from Luke 17, where ten lepers are healed and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Jesus. The day sits easily with Catholic life, since the word Eucharist comes from the Greek for thanksgiving.

GaudeteSunday.about: The Third Sunday of Advent is called Gaudete Sunday, from the first words of its entrance antiphon in Latin, “Gaudete in Domino semper”, which means “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4). With Advent more than half over, the Church pauses in its waiting to rejoice that the Lord is near. For this reason the priest may wear rose vestments in place of violet, and the third candle of the Advent wreath is commonly rose as well. The Gospel turns to John the Baptist, who points to the one who is coming. Rose is used on only one other day of the year, Laetare Sunday in Lent.

LaetareSunday.about: The Fourth Sunday of Lent is called Laetare Sunday, from the opening of its entrance antiphon in Latin, “Laetare, Ierusalem”, which means “Rejoice, Jerusalem” and is taken from Isaiah 66. Coming just past the middle of Lent, it offers a moment of encouragement, since Easter is now in sight. The priest may wear rose vestments in place of violet, and on this day the altar may be decorated with flowers and the organ played more freely, both of which are otherwise set aside in Lent. In Britain and Ireland the day is also kept as Mothering Sunday. Rose is otherwise worn only on Gaudete Sunday in Advent.

EasterOctave.about: The eight days from Easter Sunday to the Second Sunday of Easter form the Easter octave, and the Church keeps each of them with the rank of a solemnity, as though Easter Day were prolonged. At Mass the Gloria is said every day, the Easter sequence may be repeated, and the dismissal ends with a double Alleluia. The Gospels go through the appearances of the risen Lord one by one: to Mary Magdalene, to the disciples on the road to Emmaus, in the upper room, and by the Sea of Galilee. In the early Church the newly baptised wore their white garments throughout this week.

ChristmasOctave.about: The eight days from 25 December to 1 January make up the Christmas octave. The Gloria is said at Mass each day. The first days bring three old feasts: Saint Stephen, the first martyr, on 26 December, Saint John the Apostle on the 27th, and the Holy Innocents, the children killed by Herod, on the 28th. They show from the start that the child in the manger is to be followed at a cost. The days that remain continue the Gospel of the infancy, with Simeon and Anna in the Temple, and the octave closes on the solemnity of Mary, Mother of God.

HolyWeekWeekday.about: Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week are the last full days of Lent, and no saint’s day may take their place. The Gospels follow the days before the Passion. On Monday Mary of Bethany anoints the feet of Jesus. On Tuesday Jesus foretells that Judas will betray him and Peter deny him. On Wednesday, sometimes called Spy Wednesday, Judas agrees with the chief priests on thirty pieces of silver. The first readings are taken from Isaiah’s songs of the suffering Servant. In many dioceses the Chrism Mass is celebrated on one of these days. They are good days for confession before the Triduum begins.

OAntiphons.about: From 17 to 24 December Advent enters its final stage, and the weekday Masses tell from Matthew and Luke the events that led up to the birth of Christ. These days take their popular name from the seven “O Antiphons” sung with the Magnificat at Evening Prayer from 17 to 23 December, and used as the Alleluia verse at Mass. In use since at least the eighth century, each calls on Christ to come, addressing him by an Old Testament title: Wisdom, Adonai, Root of Jesse, Key of David, Rising Dawn, King of the Nations, Emmanuel. The hymn “O come, O come, Emmanuel” is based on them.
